subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I announced in the house on March 8,
1957, the Canadian and United States officials had preliminary talks on March 19, 1957, on the subject of waters which cross the boundary between our two countries.
The purpose of the meeting was to consider the steps required to organize effectively the main talks. There was a full and, I may add, a very satisfactory exchange of views. The terms of reference for the discussions were drawn up. These are being submitted to each government for their consideration.
As a result of the March 19 meeting and of subsequent consideration it is hoped that the first meeting for these talks will be held in Washington in May of this year. I expect personally to head the Canadian delegation. At this meeting we will begin to get into the substance of the discussions.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: May I ask the minister if a representative of the province of British Columbia will be included in these talks?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the preliminary meeting held in Ottawa on March 19 there were representatives only of the United States and Canadian governments. However, there was one representative, or possibly two, of the government of British Columbia in Ottawa at the time for consultation with our own officials. Consultation was held with them and it was found very useful. If the government of British Columbia wishes to send representatives with the Canadian delegation to Washington in May in order that we may consult them as the talks proceed, they will be most welcome.

On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
May I ask
the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources a further question in connection with the negotiations between the Canadian government and the United States government on the question of downstream benefits from water storage on the Columbia river. To what extent has the Canadian position been weakened by the publicly announced position of the Minister of Fisheries, repeated recently in Vancouver, indicating that he is opposed to the diversion of Columbia river waters into the Fraser river system?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member should read in Hansard what I said three days ago on that very subject.

Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: I have read it, and on that basis I would like to ask the minister a supplementary question. Is it not a fact that in these negotiations one of the most powerful levers in Canada's favour in obtaining the best return for downstream benefits is the possibility of the Columbia river diversion to the Fraser, and that any suggestion that any government minister is opposed to this will weaken Canada's position?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: I have said time and again that these were diplomatic negotiations, and I do not intend at any time to discuss the substance of the subject matter in the house or in public.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: Then may I ask the Prime Minister what is the position of the right hon. gentleman with respect to the principle of cabinet solidarity, when we have one minister saying that the Columbia diversion is definitely still a possibility and another stating, in what we are told is a pronouncement of government policy, in Vancouver, that he is opposed to such a diversion?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: There is cabinet solidarity as to all decisions that are taken. There need not be cabinet solidarity about each individual minister's opinions on for example some of the questions that are asked.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: I was asking the Prime Minister not about an expression of opinion but about a press release which we were told in this house represented government policy, and which was made in the form of an announcement, not in answer to a question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: I think this debate has gone far enough at this point.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources a question arising out of his statement earlier this afternoon about the negotiations concerning the international rivers.
Is the federal aid policy which was announced on March 26 subject to the prior completion of an agreement between Canada and the United States? It would appear from the wording of the announcement that this is to be the case, but if so, I am wondering why there should be that restriction on the policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have nothing to add to what I already said in the house when I read the statement made by the Minister of Fisheries.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Are we to take it then that the policy announced by the Minister of Fisheries
[Mr. Lesage.)

is subject to the completion of an agreement between Canada and the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have nothing to add and I will not be brought into a discussion of what exactly is meant by a sentence or two sentences. The document speaks for itself..

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: That is a very poor answer. You can surely do better than that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this brings up the question of the South Saskatchewan dam. In view of what is being done now and the complete change of face on the part of the government in respect to assistance for the production of power, thus removing their major objection to proceeding with the South Saskatchewan project, is the Prime Minister in a position to say that this will now be proceeded with?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext:
No, I am not going to say it is
going to be proceeded with, because it is not regarded as a self-supporting or self-liquidating scheme. What has been done is to suggest to the authorities of the Atlantic provinces that something could be done similar to the creation and ownership of the northern Ontario pipe line, provided it was agreeable to them that the Canadian government should proceed in that fashion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext:
The Prime Minister uses as an excuse the fact that if this dam were proceeded with it would mean that the federal
Inquiries of the Ministry government was participating in a power development. The fact is that one of the reasons this could not be proceeded with was that it would mean that the federal government was participating in the production of power. That is now something that has been changed first by the Minister of Fisheries in a British Columbia announcement and also by a budget announcement. Is there going to be reconsideration now of the South Saskatchewan dam?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext: There is reconsideration of all these projects, and I have declared time and again that I would not take the responsibility of recommending to parliament that this scheme be proceeded with until I was convinced it was something that would put back into the whole national economy more than it would take out annually in the form of interest and amortization charges; and I have not yet been able to become convinced that such would be the case.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext: I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question supplementary to those put to him about the South Saskatchewan river project. Would the Prime Minister not consider proceeding with the project even though he may feel it is not entirely self-liquidating, in view of the fact that the government was prepared to proceed with the northern Ontario gas pipe line even though it was not clear at the time that it would be self-liquidating?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government was of the opinion that that would be self-liquidating. There may have been some uncertainty with regard to the time by which it was felt it would become so, but there was no doubt that it would ultimately be self-liquidating.
With respect to the South Saskatchewan river scheme, I am personally impressed by the fact that there are apt to be indirect benefits which it is very difficult to appraise at this moment, but these, in my judgment, will be taken into account in any further reconsideration that is given to this project.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister prepared to give reconsideration to the project during the current session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext: The Prime Minister cannot extend any hope to any hon. member, no matter how many questions are asked, that an affirmative decision will be reached in the course of this session, nor in the course of the next few weeks.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN PROJECT
speechtext:
Up to June 12?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 25 a question was directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concerning a serious charge made by Arthur Blakely in that morning's

Montreal Gazette to the effect that the government is interfering in C.B.C. public affairs programs. Subsequently I asked the minister whether there had been any correspondence between the Prime Minister or any other minister and Mr. A. Davidson Dunton, chairman of the board of directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The Minister of National Revenue then interjected that he personally had not had any such correspondence. Then I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare if he would ascertain whether the Prime Minister or any minister of the government had such correspondence, to which I received this reply:
I shall take notice of my hon. friend's question and direct it to the attention of the Prime Minister when he returns.
Perhaps the Prime Minister could answer that question today.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
After I had been in the house yesterday afternoon my attention was called to an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette, I think it was on Monday, March 25, and so far as it concerns me it is absolutely inaccurate. I have not attempted to interfere in any of the manners suggested.
I do not think I should ask my colleagues if they have had any correspondence with Mr. Dunton. There certainly has been no correspondence with Mr. Dunton authorized by the government.
I did have some correspondence with Mr. Dunton in October about something which has nothing at all to do with partisan politics, in which I wrote him, not as Prime Minister but as a Canadian citizen, about the tone of a broadcast I had heard. I suggested I thought it was not a proper use of funds appropriated by parliament to provide fees for broadcasts of that character.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister be willing to table that letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
No, I would not, sir.	I would have no objection to
showing my hon. friend the correspondence but I would not like to set a precedent that correspondence between a member of the government and someone who happens to be in any one of these crown agencies should be tabled.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
In view of the fact that it is very difficult for the Prime Minister to bifurcate himself into being Prime Minister at one moment and private citizen at the other, would he reveal the nature of his complaint? What was said or done that offended his sensibilities?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: I think at the time there had been two broadcasts by a young gentleman from abroad who was presented as a Canadian university professor, and who expressed very profound views upon international affairs in a tone of persiflage that I thought it was not fitting to have used in that way. The answer I got was, well, the C.B.C. tries to provide an opportunity for every view to be expressed. To that I rejoined that this might be all right if the young gentleman in question had been introduced in a manner that made his identity appreciated, but that being a Canadian university professor retained to expound views on the C.B.C., the public may very well arrive at the conclusion that these were views sponsored by this agency of the Canadian public, and I did not think that was a proper attitude to which an agency should apply funds appropriated at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister believe that he should be directing any selective decisions as to who should speak?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
No, but the
Prime Minister believes that any Canadian citizen is entitled to write to the C.B.C. and express his views as he conceives them to be, about the propriety of some of the broadcasts that are made at the cost of the Canadian taxpayer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Did the Prime Minister write this private letter on the Prime Minister's stationery, and did he say he was writing as a private citizen? This is a very serious interference with the C.B.C.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: I have not the sheet of paper on which my letter was written, and the carbon copy I have does not show whether or not it was written on official stationery.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: You do not even know if you wrote it on government paper.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Did the young professor referred to happen to be pointing out to the Canadian public the many shortcomings of this government?

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Was the young professor referred to in this case pointing out to the Canadian public the many shortcomings of his own government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
No; he was
referring to the timidity of the Canadian nation and its fear of getting its little toes burned.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister what specific steps he took, if any, to make it clear to Mr. Dunton that this protest came from him personally and that it did not have behind it his weight as Prime Minister of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: I took no special steps in that regard.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: May I put a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Since he has now made known the fact that he wrote this letter, and in view of the fact that he is Prime Minister and probably wrote it as Prime Minister, does he not feel that the correspondence should be tabled?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
No. I do
not think that kind of precedent should be established, but if the hon. gentleman wishes to see the letter I would be glad to show it to him, and I will not ask him to refrain from taking any responsibility he feels he should take after he has seen it. I extend the same offer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Order; the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: With respect to the Prime Minister's reference to a precedent, what does he think of the precedent he has established in writing this letter at all?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
I do not
think that was any new precedent. I would imagine that hundreds of letters are written to the C.B.C. in respect of matters such as the one I wrote him about.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Hundreds by prime ministers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Well, no; there happens to be only one prime minister at this time, and I have written, well, two letters. There was one letter, an answer from Mr. Dunton, and a reply to Mr. Dun-ton's letter.

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister not think the only fair way to handle this letter now would be to have it tabled, rather than to place the onus on the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself with respect to the disclosure of the contents of the letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: No. I have disclosed no other names but my name and that of Mr. Dunton.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: You disclosed the young professor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wishes to see the correspondence and wishes to take the responsibility of-

subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: It should not be my responsibility.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
It is not
going to be mine.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question. Does what the Prime Minister has now admitted not confirm in part Mr. Blakely's charge?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: No, it does not, sir.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: It does in the view of some of us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext: I cannot be responsible for that kind of opinion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, I take it that all questions that have to be asked this day have been asked. While some questions were being asked I found in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, citation 295, part of which reads:
A question oral or written must not-
There are several paragraphs which indicate what type of question should not be asked. I found some of these paragraphs very interesting. For instance, paragraph (c) reads:
A question oral or written must not:
(c)	multiply, with slight variations, a similar question on the same point.
(d)	repeat in substance a question already answered, or to which an answer has been refused.
(e)	inquire whether statements made in a newspaper are true.
(f)	contain an expression of opinion.
(j)	be framed so as to suggest its own answer.
(k)	be a speech, however short; nor be of unreasonable length.
(s) embody a series of questions which should be moved for by an address or order.
(w) raise a matter of policy too large to be dealt with in the limits of an answer to a question.
(bb) ask the government's opinion on matters of policy.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo).

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the views of the opposition in regard to the budget have been

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker set forth by the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Eglinton in particular, and by other hon. members who have spoken. I do not intend today to repeat the matters they dealt with, but rather to examine in general the circumstances under which the governor of the Bank of Canada made his recent announcement, and also to place before the house the stand which the official opposition intends to take on the C.C.F. subamendment.
As far as old age pensions are concerned, we believe the increase is totally inadequate for the needy; it is niggardly and paltry. Twenty cents a day will do nothing to help the needy among the old age pensioners of this nation. The increase of $6 per month simply will not meet their desperate need; and with the government spending so extravagantly and so profligately in other directions there are no words with which one could describe its disregard of the needs of our senior citizens.
With regard to the removal of the taxes on candy and soft drinks, may I say that the tax on soft drinks has needed to be removed for several years because the increasing cost of production has made it necessary that this action be taken. However, it must not be forgotten that this is an election year and that some of these changes have been made before. If the unhappy occurrence takes place and this government is re-elected, the experience of the past would indicate that while this type of reduction generally takes place in an election year by pure coincidence, after the election the taxes have been reimposed with the return of the government.
It is well to remember that the 25 per cent tax on soft drinks was repealed in March 1949, with an election in June of that year. It is also well to remember that it was restored and increased in September, 1950, and reduced to 15 per cent in April, 1952. The 30 per cent ad valorem tax on candy and confectionery was removed in March,
1949,	placed back as a tax at 30 per cent in
1950,	and then later on reduced to 15 per cent. The same situation prevailed with respect to the tax on electric refrigerators. It was off in 1945, an election year, and on again in 1947; it was off in 1948, and back at 15 per cent in 1951. In any of these cases I am not dealing with changes that have take place since. In the case of automobiles, the tax was reduced from 25 per cent to 10 per cent on May 14, 1945, with an election in June of that year. It was increased to 25 per cent on November 17, 1947, and so on during the years that followed.
In other words these changes are in keeping with certain other changes which were

made on previous occasions. I know the excuse will be made that the extra taxation in 1950 was because of the Korean crisis which faced this nation, but that does not explain the other examples to which I have made reference, nor is it an adequate answer to what happened in 1950.
As I read this budget and the observations thereon on the part of the minister and of Mr. Coyne in his annual report, they present to me a most bewildering exposition of government policy. In his budget speech on March 14 the Minister of Finance is reported on page 2216 of Hansard as saying:
Meanwhile, the economy has kept on a fairly even keel, despite the speed of its advance, and prices and living costs have advanced only moderately. To have achieved such expansion with so little disorganization is, I think, a source of satisfaction.
I underline the words "and prices and living costs have advanced only moderately". The minister continued:
I come now to consider the economic prospects for the coming fiscal year. On the present evidence I think we can expect a continuation of the current high level of economic activity throughout the coming year. There may, as always, he some unevenness between industries and regions, but by and large I expect the momentum of expansion to continue, at a somewhat more moderate pace but strongly enough to ensure further increases in production and employment, and a continuation of rising standards of living.
I find support for this in the information released a few weeks ago by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to investment intentions for the coming year.
This poses immediately another question, and that question is this. Whose opinion will you accept? Here is what Mr. Coyne had to say in his annual report:
I believe that total spending of all kinds in 1956-the combination of capital expenditures, personal consumption expenditures and government expenditures, domestic expenditures as well as expenditures for imports-was at least $1 billion greater than would have been desirable from the point of view of general stability and sound economic growth.
The stand taken by the government has been this. Some of the ministers have denied that there is inflation, while others have pointed out the dangers of inflation. Telling the people not to spend would be more convincing, Mr. Speaker, if the government practised what it preaches. In other words, in 1956 and 1957 this government will establish an all-time high in expenditures apart altogether from the old age security fund operations, which are financed by separate taxes. The Minister of Finance would make a greater appeal to this nation if he would say, "Do as I do" rather than as is the case today, "Do as I say, don't do as I do."
After all, the governor of the Bank of Canada has pointed out again and again

the extraordinarily large expenditure which is being undertaken on the part of the government, but there has been no serious attempt by the government to reduce unnecessary and wasteful expenditure. They have continued their policy of spending and high taxation. When we, on the part of the opposition, endeavoured to secure the setting up of a committee similar to the Hoover commission in the United States to investigate and recommend reductions, such a committee, though successful in the United States, was not permitted here.
This could not have been because this government is opposed to royal commissions, for it has set up more commissions in recent years than any government in living memory. This government refused the suggestion of the opposition that the committee on estimates should have the power to call witnesses and have documents produced, though that committee could operate successfully only with its members having the right to have witnesses brought before them, rather than selected witnesses chosen by the government for its own purposes.
I ask, too, what is the general policy of this government regarding taxation. In 1949 Mr. Abbott said in his budget speech:
We must recognize that most Canadians, like other people in recent years, have shown they prefer to pay taxes in a form other than high income taxes.
Mr. Abbott cut the income tax that year. He repealed certain indirect taxes, and reduced corporation taxes. That was an election year. In 1953 he cut income tax rates, reduced some corporation taxes, removed the radio tax, the stamp tax and taxes on certain other commodities. He expressed the view at that time that the way to secure greater production was to reduce income tax, and that such a course would combat inflation.
I ask the Minister of Finance when this change came about on the part of this government. After all, many of the ministers of the present government belonged to that government when Mr. Abbott enunciated that policy as a means of meeting inflation. My hori. friend from Eglinton points out that the Minister of Finance was a member of that government and naturally, with cabinet solidarity being what it is, he must have accepted that general principle which was enunciated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As usual the hon. gentleman
is wrong. I did not join the government until January, 1950.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am subject to correction in that regard. But whatever the date upon which the present Minister of Finance came into the government, that same
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker policy was followed until he became minister. Whatever the case may be-and I accept the hori. gentleman's statement, naturally-the fact remains that following his achievement of cabinet rank that same policy was followed, and I quote this particularly from Mr. Abbott's remarks at the time:
Income tax rates, if too high, can do harm in many directions. Tax laws should avoid placing too great a penalty on successful effort. Every reasonable incentive should be given to people to work hard, take risks and expand their businesses without keeping one eye on the tax gatherer. This is particularly important in a country such as ours which is growing and expanding.
Indeed, the Minister of Finance himself, when he did become minister, made a speech in the city of Montreal as reported on December 17, 1954, in which he said that the situation regarding taxation'-the height of taxation-and the degree to which it interfered with effort and initiative was, to use his own words, "amazing". "I am amazed", he said. Those were his words at that time. However, each of these ministers cannot be right.
Taxes are too high today. Taxes are interfering with production. Taxes are preventing the production without which inflation cannot be met. Yet when we take the view that a reduction in income tax is necessary, supporters of the government ridicule the idea and say it is not in keeping with responsibility, having regard to present inflationary trends. I call as witness in that regard one of our greatest tax gatherers since Matthew, and I refer to B. W. Scully, a former deputy minister in charge of income tax who, now in business, reveals his views regarding Canadian income tax and its effects on the Canadian people. He says:
Money desperately needed for planned expansion is being siphoned away from corporations and individuals. This has become a vicious and chronic habit with our government. It is one that could some day bring about the end of this system of free enterprise which has enabled all of us to prosper as we have.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we find ourselves in a position where Canadian corporations are denied an equal opportunity with United States corporations in Canada with regard to the investment of risk capital. Why has this legislation not been changed? Why has the deterrent to Canadian investment in risk enterprises not been removed from the income tax laws? Why should we in Canada find ourselves in a position where United States corporations can engage in risk enterprises in expanding and developing our resources, and do so on better terms than can Canadians? These are questions that Canadians are asking.

The Budget-Mr. Diejenbaker
Maybe, however, that comes of the indirect way in which taxation is imposed. Due to the fact that the major portion is deducted at the source, Canadians have not realized how heavily they are taxed. In the United States today there is a tremendous public movement on the part of people outraged at the levels of taxation, demanding reductions and securing reductions. Yet in the United States we fin'd that the income of the average American, after taxes are paid, is nearly 30 per cent higher than that of the average Canadian after taxation. The Hamilton Spectator summarizes the situation regarding our taxation in this land iri these words:
The politicians know that payroll deductions and other apparently painless taxes have transformed taxation from a historic annoyance into a hazy narcotic.
A sinister illusion is growing that climbing income and corporation taxes somehow are coming out of a great and limitless pocket divorced from the man on the street and the housewife-a serious, even tragic, misconception.
I know that in certain quarters it is popular to advocate increasing taxation as against corporations, to say that further taxation as against corporations is needed. I say to those who hold that view that our present rates of taxation are denying reinvestment and expansion and are in part responsible for the degree to which United States investment is taking over control of many of the major industries in this nation.
In order to show that his surplus was not as large as it actually was the minister engaged in the juggling referred to at length by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). By the allocation of over $150 million the minister was able to reduce the amount of the surplus and thereby endeavour to show the Canadian people that they were overtaxed less than they actually were. Having successfully done that this year, we find that he intends to follow the same course next year, in other words, to juggle his accounts so that the actual surplus will not be shown. As found at page 2221 of Hansard of March 14, the minister said:
... I propose for the coming year that a further $50 million be credited to the reserve against assets, bringing it up to about $600 million against total assets of about $8 billion. I am also proposing to appropriate another $50 million to reduce the unamortized deficit in our superannuation account to $89 million. In addition, early in the new fiscal year we shall be paying over to the Canada council if royal assent is given to the bill the amount of $100 million.
It is the same old play, concealment of the actual facts, concealment of the fact that overtaxation today is placing Canadians in a position detrimental to the future of the country and is defeating the very purpose that is put forward for the existence of this
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
overtaxation, namely, that it is designed to meet inflation. Apparently the basis upon, which the budget is founded is that Canadians cannot be trusted to spend their own money. If they spend their own money that makes inflation, but when the government takes it from them and engages in the greatest spending in all history, with the exception of one year during the days of the war, such spending does no harm.
I say to the government, "If you would meet inflation, physician, heal yourself." Let us have some action on the part of the government to bring about the reduction of unnecessary expenditure. As a matter of fact, the high rates of personal and corporate taxation mean that the incentive to produce is sacrificed, that as a consequence manufacturing costs are on the rise and that we find ourselves challenged in our markets in every part of the world.
The Winnipeg Tribune discussed the matter at some length and pointed out that what was actually done in the present budget was to pretend to fight inflation and at the same time to give some indication by a general spread of benefits that the voters might be disposed to support the government. You ask Canadians to check inflation. When did you find out it existed? When did it begin? In 1955 you were encouraging inflation by your policies, and then in 1956 you began to realize that by gradual steps inflation was taking place. What of 1957? We find expenditures amounting to $5,018 million and revenues estimated to be $5,170 million. The Regina Leader-Post, which has not been a severe critic of the government in the past, has summarized the anomalous situation of the government in these words:
The major quarrel with the budget arises from Mr. Harris' admonition that the people should spend less and save more, a device which Mr. Harris and the federal government are failing to put into practice . . .
The Bank of Canada warns that a 3 per cent rise in consumer prices in seven months is disturbing and would certainly be dangerous if it were to continue at the same rate. The governor of the bank has warned the government. The government saw his report before it was produced here. He warned them about government expenditures and the need to take action to reduce them. Yet instead of taking action the government fans the fires of inflation by failing to restrict its own expenditures. Indeed, the major creator of the existing inflation is the actions of this government.
I intend to deal generally for a moment with the problem of inflation. The Bank of Canada cannot preserve the cake if the government spending departments insist on eating

it. That was an editorial comment in one of the papers of this country and it summarizes the situation. Physician, heal thyself. The government asks Canadians to draw in their belts while it continues its orgy of expenditure and takes from Canadians $24 to $35 more per person in taxation than is needed for the costs of government.
Inflation will not be met by forcing the provinces and municipalities to increase their costs. According to the figures given by the minister, last year they had to borrow $772 million in new bond issues. Cities across the nation find themselves actually in a position where the costs of borrowing are making it impossible for them to carry on the ordinary and requisite expenditures to meet an ever-increasing population.
What is the government going to do about it? What action does the government intend to take? It superintended the imposition of higher interest rates. It refuses to reduce its wasteful expenditure. It refuses, as I said a moment ago, to permit the setting up of either a commission or committees to recommend action. All of us agree with the objective, namely, that this situation must be met. The only difference between us is that we do not believe it can be met with a government that persists in spending and increasing its expenditures without regard to the effects of these increases.
Credit restrictions? Did they prevent inflation? According to the governor of the Bank of Canada they did not and if the increase in consumer costs in the last few months persists the situation will be dangerous. We find that housing has practically been undermined in this nation or was until the 7th of March, with major projects being shelved by municipalities and with the economy of various parts of the nation frozen at a lower level than the economy of other parts.
Those are things which the people of this nation realize. Those are things which this government does not realize because it places the responsibility for action everywhere but on its own doorstep. I believe that all of us must take a responsible attitude towards meeting this grave danger and, unless action is taken, it will threaten the stability of our economy. All of us recognize that in addition to government spending, consumer and investment spending contributes to the total spending and thus adds to the pressure of demand upon productive capacity. I repeat this, and it cannot be too often repeated, the government refuses to accept for itself the medicine that it prescribes for others. While refusing to cut its own spending, while exhorting banking institutions to exercise restraint in extending consumer
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker credit, it has adopted a monetary policy which has placed almost the whole burden of restraint on the investment sector. This restraint has been felt by all small businesses in this nation, for it is the small and medium-size businesses which have been forced to the wall as a result of this policy, ineffective as it has been.
What have been the weaknesses of government policy? First, it has attacked inflation by attacking the volume of investment and by reducing the rate of economic growth. This, to me, is unsound, since inflation by description is not due to too much production but to too little. It has enhanced the competitive power of large business as against the small business man, with agriculture and particularly prairie agriculture being a special sufferer. It exercised no noticeable restraint on many types of less essential spending, while severely restricting investment in social capital, as I mentioned a moment ago for example, in needed municipal development and in the crucial field of housing. It has also clearly resulted in regional discrimination. The maritimes have been particularly discriminated against in this regard. It has attempted to solve a dangerous situation almost solely by monetary policy, despite the technical limitations which have been shown in the experiences of the last few months. These limitations have been repeatedly pointed out by the presidents of the various chartered banks and are now admitted by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
No one denies that there is no painless cure for inflation. We have to cut down total spending when total spending exceeds our productive capacity. Cuts are imperative. Again, I say it is the government itself that must act. If it makes a determined and effectual effort to reduce its own spending and inflationary forces still persist it would be the task of government to consider whether less essential consumer spending should be given consideration. Up to the present, in all too many cases, exactly the reverse has been happening. Capital investment maintains our economic growth, supports our welfare expenditures and makes possible the contribution that we make to social security measures as well as providing for full employment. Yet, because of political expediency and technically using and implementing a policy of general monetary restraint, it is precisely this sector of investment which this government has attacked. However, the attack on the investment sector has been directed or at least been effective only against the small business, and as a result has been grossly and unwisely discriminatory. I believe we should stimulate enterprise, encourage initiative and expand the rate of economic

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker growth. I believe with Mr. Abbott, in his declaration of several years ago, that the means of encouraging production is through a proper regard to the reduction of taxation which denies initiative.
We are confronted today by big government spending. We are confronted by the fact that small business, the farmer and the economical progress of the poorer provinces is being affected by this policy. Indeed, the centralization of economic power invites the undermining of the foundation of the economy. In support of that I again quote Mr. Scully, who had experience for years as the trusted confident of government departments and today has experience in business and finds that the action that ought to be taken is not being taken. Yes, the policy so far attempted, if you can call it that, condemns itself by the experiences that have followed its adoption. We condemn it, and I think the nation as a whole will condemn it. Sir, this policy is impractical in so far as effectiveness is concerned and I think unless the government itself acts to reduce its own unnecessary expenditures, it will continue to be ineffective.
I come now to the recent recommendations made by Mr. Coyne. I think that the house and the country deserve fuller information than they have been given on this matter. Apparently Mr. Coyne, with the blessing of the minister, met with the press and pointed out the need for action in connection with the banks in this country. In his report he states that in order to meet the situation created in the housing industry, as I see it, and the detrimental effects that have followed on the lumber industry of British Columbia and other parts of Canada; in order to bail out the government from the impossible position in which it found itself, he suggested the segregation of savings for mortgage purposes. Yes, it appeared when the government announced that, that indeed here was a governor with a strange device. We in the opposition think a great deal of the Bank of Canada. We know how the banking system in the late 20's and 30's weathered the storm. We know it was Mr. Bennett who decided, when he was prime minister, that there should be a banker's bank and the Bank of Canada was set up. We know that it was to direct policy and that credit should be regulated to keep the economy on an even keel. We know, too, the experience of 1929 and 1930, when the United States banks operated on the basis of advancing money on real estate and when the call came on the part of the depositors they were unable to meet it and went into bankruptcy, so the depositors lost in every part of the nation.

Our banks were traditionally not allowed to enter the mortgage money-lending field. They were pushed into that field. The tight-money situation, which the Minister of Finance now talks about, pushed the banks out of that field for a moment, or for a short period of time during the early months of this year, and then came this novel suggestion, as I have said, that the savings of Canadians are to be pushed into the real estate long-term field, if those recommendations are accepted.
Canada has always been proud of its banking system; it is the envy of people everywhere. I want to view Mr. Coyne's recommendations with objectivity. On the other hand, I do not want to see the public institutions of credit of this nation used as an instrument by the government. I believe that if those plans were carried into effect in the form in which they have been enunciated they would reduce the bankers of this country to a group of sycophants answerable to the government. That to me is a step that should not be taken without grave consideration and decision on the part of the Canadian people as a whole.
The government found itself embarrassed by its tight-money policy, because that policy resulted in a practical cessation of housebuilding and the assigning of housing loans. Then it was that Mr. Coyne made his announcement; then it was that questions were asked in the house; then it was that there was criticism on the part of the president of the Bank of Montreal. The major support the government got for these suggestions was the promised support of the C.C.F. party, which fully endorsed the recommendations which were made.
We endeavoured to get information. The answers given by the minister in no way clarify the situation whatsoever. All they do is postpone any decision until after the election, because the government did not want to take any stand on this matter before the election, hoping against the improbable event of being returned to power and then to act. The Canadian people have the right to have information in this regard, not the uncertain information that the minister gave on March 26. When questions were asked by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) the minister read a prepared statement, and he finally ended up by saying this:
In any case no "radical", "fundamental" or "precipitate" actions relating to the structure of Canadian banking have been suggested, nor are they contemplated by the government.
That is a long way from saying that the government does not intend, if it is returned to power, to do this very thing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance on bringing down one of the most sound, honest and courageous budgets we have had in this country for many years. Before continuing with my remarks I should like to refer to a statement made just a few moments ago by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition paid a great tribute to the Tory members sitting in this house who come from New Brunswick. He was indicating to the house and to the general public that the only members from the maritime provinces who are trying to do anything for the citizens of the maritime provinces are those Conservative members who come from that area. It is most pleasing for me to note that in his budget the minister has introduced the very

suggestions that we Liberal members from the maritime provinces have made. Every matter in the budget which is beneficial to our part of the country was brought to the attention of the minister by Liberal members from the maritimes.
These improvements, I realize, are most harmful to the Tory party at this time. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has just come back irom the maritime provinces, and I believe he came back most disillusioned after he had found out about the way in which this budget had been received in that area. I do not believe it gave him very much encouragement, because, if ever there was a budget which was designed to assist the citizens of the maritime provinces it was the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance a few days ago.
There are many other benefits contained in that budget which will be most helpful not only to the citizens of the maritime provinces but to all Canadians. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) when he spoke immediately after the budget had been brought down the other evening, had this to say at page 2250 of Hansard.
A great deal of what has been done is for the benefit of the people who are able to help themselves.
I wonder if when the hon. member for Greenwood made that statement he was referring to the people of the maritime provinces. Was he referring to the old age pensioners, to those receiving old age assistance, to those receiving blind disability pensions, or to war disabled pensioners in receipt of federal aid? Was he referring to family allowances, to the deduction in respect of medical costs, charitable gifts and so on; or was he referring to the removal of the 10 per cent tax on tea, coffee and other foods which every housewife has to buy?
My thought is that the hon. member for Greenwood was very much disturbed to find that there had been no change in income tax rates which, of course, if reduced, usually provide much greater benefits to those in the higher income brackets. The Leader of the Opposition, when he was speaking this afternoon, made some comparisons between taxation in the United States and taxation in Canada. The hon. member for Greenwood did exactly the same thing when he spoke, and he was most critical of the fact that there had been no tax reductions in the budget just brought down, although they both seemed to think that it was an election budget.
That is why I call this a courageous budget on the part of the Minister of Finance. I believe it might be well at this particular

period to put some figures on the record which will authenticate this comparison between the tax rate in this country and that of other democratic countries, all expressed in terms of Canadian dollars. A single man in Canada gets an exemption of $1,000. His counterpart in Australia gets an exemption of $224, and he must pay tax on any income in excess of that. In the United Kingdom a single man would pay tax on any amount above $385, while in the great and rich country to the south of us, the United States, he would pay tax on everything over $600.
Thus, we allow under our tax law a difference of 40 per cent before we begin to calculate income tax at all-$1,000 in Canada as compared with $600 in the United States. It is in a situation like this that the Leader of the Opposition today swung his arms in great anger about the tax structure in this country being so unfair as compared with that of other countries in the world. Now I would like to put on the record Mr. Speaker, a few more comparisons with regard to married men. In this country a married man gets an exemption of $2,000, while in the United States, which has the highest exemption figure of comparable countries, it is $1,200. In the United Kingdom it is $660, and in Australia $447. These figures, I believe, clearly indicate that no country in the world has a better tax system than this country of ours, or one that is more fair to the people.
I come now to a matter that I am called upon to deal with quite frequently-I refer to the provincial government in New Brunswick, and the Progressive Conservative members in Ottawa who are determined to convince the citizens of our province and of other parts of the country that all the troubles in New Brunswick, and all their tribulations, can be placed on the doorstep of the federal government. The legislature opened in New Brunswick a few weeks ago. Our premier opened the debate on the speech from the throne, and half the time taken up in that debate was spent in criticism of the actions of the federal government toward the province of New Brunswick. A few days later, the debate was ended, and the premier closed the debate, using exactly the same terms, exactly the same criticism, and aiming at the same target-the federal government.
When the budget in New Brunswick was brought down a few days ago, the secretary treasurer started off like this:
New Brunswick needs more federal aid if it is to improve its relative economic position.
We have heard a lot this afternoon about the expenditures of this federal government.
The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart The headlines in the same paper which reported those words read: "New Brunswick Budgets for a Record $64 million".
The approach of the Progressive Conservative party just prior to an election is exactly the same as the approach in every province where they are trying to defeat the government in power. They have a greater policy of economy, but the minute they are in the driver's seat they spend more money than was ever known before in the history of that province. When the government of New Brunswick took over in 1952, our total revenue was $52 million. This has been increased to $64 million through the generosity of this government. And still they are begging for more. Yet every bit of their trouble is placed on the doorstep of the federal government. I believe this is most unfair and I believe it is something we must face and deal with as federal members.
The premier of our province also said in his remarks that the rehabilitation and growth of the Atlantic provinces could not be achieved through small federal expenditures. I have yet to hear the premier of our province or any tory member ever make any mention of Camp Gagetown which is one of the biggest projects under construction in this country today. I have yet to hear one of them make a complimentary remark about it and may I say for the sake of comparison, that the cost of Camp Gagetown will be five times greater than the cost of the causeway in Nova Scotia. There will be 2,000 employees the year round at Gagetown, and an annual payroll of about $15 million. The project will lead to the creation of a town of between 12,000 and 15,000 population. I wonder if the tory members from New Brunswick could indicate any industries there which are employing so many employees with so large a payroll.
I might add that this project is taking place right on the premier's doorstep, and that he must know all about it. But he has not said one word about the fact that this is one of the greatest projects that ever came to our province; and I would like any hon. member here to tell me if he has heard anyone pay it a single compliment. To give the house some idea of the magnitude of this undertaking, may I point out that some time ago I asked how many houses had been subject to a federal government contract, how many had been completed, and so on. I found that 143 houses have been completed, 597 were under construction, and that 324 are to be started in the near future, giving a total of 1,059.

The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart
Well, Mr. Speaker, no mention has been made of this important project, to be completed at a cost five times greater than that of the causeway-a cost about one-third as large as the whole of the Canadian expenditure in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway. However, not a Conservative in my province has a good word to say for it, though it is one of the greatest benefits that has ever come to the province. Nevertheless, we, as Liberal members, welcome it.
I also realize that when I stand up as a Liberal and contradict anything that has been said by a tory member from our province, I am accused of being a saboteur, of being disloyal, and of many other things which are not too complimentary. It would seem that the tory members from that province feel that they are here to do nothing but criticize, and that no one who defends the government should come here as a Liberal member. I feel, however, that I have that part to play, and when I believe that the government is right I support it and, of course, that is at all times. I do not intend to sit here and listen to abuse and condemnation of a government which has done so much for my province.
Another matter I would like to mention briefly is the fact that Conservatives try to make the people in my province believe that if they did ever form a government here in Ottawa they would make things much easier for us in the maritime provinces. Hon. members know, without my telling them, what benefits we have received from the federal government in my province. Because the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) has questioned these figures on other occasions, I think it might be well for me to put them on the record at this time. A few moments ago the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) said that provincial governments of a different political faith do not receive consideration by the federal government. The figures I have are authentic and they are for the year 1955-56. In that year the federal government took $45,227,000 in tax revenues from the province of New Brunswick. That was the total amount of taxation taken by the federal government. I am going to give the break-down of the total, but I want to put the total on the record now. In that same year the federal government paid into the province of New Brunswick $126,937,000. I cannot see how any fair-minded person could say that is a niggardly way to treat my province and I cannot agree with anyone who says that.
Let me give the figures for that period for the expenditures by the federal government represented by payments to or expenditures

That is the amount paid into the province of New Brunswick by the federal government over that 12 month period and in that same 12 month period they took out a little over $45 million. Some members may try to convince me that the government is unfair and is not treating the citizens of my province as fairly as they should be treated but in my opinion those figures are the answer. I think they also apply to the assertion made by the Leader of the Opposition when he said that

governments that are not in line with the federal government are not treated fairly.
Another statement that is often made is that if we had a Tory government at Ottawa conditions in the maritimes would be improved. I often wonder whether those from the maritimes who make such statements really believe them themselves. We all know exactly where the premiers of Quebec and Ontario have stood for years so far as the tax rental agreements are concerned. We all know, if we want to be fair, what a benefit they are to our province. I do not believe there is a Conservative member in the chamber who believes that if we had a Conservative government at Ottawa today the premiers of Quebec and Ontario would be any more willing to share any more of their wealth with us than we are receiving at the present time. I fear greatly that the situation would be just the other way around. I believe that the people of New Brunswick realize that these agreements are their only hope of survival.
As I stated a few minutes ago, federal payments to the province of New Brunswick have increased by about $8 million since 1952. The sum of $8 million means much to the government of New Brunswick and much to our people. I believe that the increases have been much more than anyone visualized five or six years ago. I know that if the premier of New Brunswick at the time when the provincial sales tax was imposed had known that these subsidy payments would be increased to such an extent we would never have had a sales tax in that province. That is why I say that the government we have there today had every reason to remove the sales tax because revenues were increased to the extent that it could have been removed with little difficulty.
When the hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) spoke in this debate they referred to broken election promises. I should like to remind the hon. members of broken election promises in my province. We were told in 1952 that the sales tax would be eliminated, that there would be a great reduction in government spending, that the department of public works would call for public tenders for all work under that department, that there would be a reduction in employees in government garages and other government services. Then, a year ago they passed a bill very hurriedly to take care of hospital insurance. At that time the premier announced that they had to get the bill through the legislature immediately in order that they might take part in the plan with the federal government.
The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart Of course, that was just before the provincial election. The bill was passed unanimously. There was not a dissenting voice. But the election took place in the meantime and the bill has not been heard of at all since. I believe that the people of New Brunswick are expecting that our premier will see fit to play his part and enter into the hospital agreement which means so much to the people of New Brunswick.
I also remember that at that particular period previous to the election there was discussion about a bridge to be built between Campobello island and Lubec, Maine. Our premier was very anxious to get the engineers of the federal Department of Public Works down there to look over the situation. He was in great haste. He wanted to get the bridge under construction as soon as possible. The provincial government got the data they felt was necessary in order to arrive at the estimated cost, but from that time on it has been a dead issue. Every effort is being made today by the federal government and the state of Maine to try to get some action but it is just impossible, and the premier of our province has refused to pay any part of the cost of the proposed bridge.
After the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) replied to a question asked by the hon. member for Royal the other day, the hon. member for Royal said that he wished to know if the figures used with respect to New Brunswick compared with Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Apparently the hon. member has failed to understand that liberalism means exactly the same treatment for all Canadians. There is nothing done for one province that is not done for another, and I do not understand why he would ask such a question. The tax rental agreements, for example, are open to each and every province and if they do not accept them that is up to them. In so far as health insurance is concerned, we are getting a better break than Ontario and Quebec in that a greater proportion of the cost is to be paid by the federal government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And less than in some other provinces.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Since the hon. member has mentioned that, I should like to go back to his speech the other night. This is what he said, as found at page 2614 of Hansard of March 22:
... I think it will take more than the eloquence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to persuade the old age pensioners who are condemned to live on their old age pensions that they should be satisfied with an increase of $6 a month.

The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart
I want to say this, that it will take more than the eloquence of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) to persuade the people of New Brunswick he has done so much for them. He failed them completely at a time when he was in a position to give them assistance, and at a time when they needed it. Old age assistance is one matter that should never be mentioned by a Tory member in the House of Commons. No one from New Brunswick should ever mention old age assistance. The record of the Conservative party in this regard is so black it covers the blackest period of history in our province, yet they have nerve enough to get up in the house here and speak about it. When they do that, it is only natural for one to sit back and say, I wonder what they would do if they were in a position to do something? That is what I want to explain.
In 1926, the hon. member for Royal and many others of his party spoke from the platform-very often when I am speaking the hon. member mentions the little red school house, and I can say he made many speeches in the little red school house. They promised the citizens of my province old age pensions and they won an election. Then, they sat back for four years, folded their arms and nothing was done.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Old age pensions were not in force in 1926.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In 1927-my memory is better than yours in that regard. In 1930 there was the grand betrayal of all time. It is the only time within my memory when the Tory party used the churches for their own benefit. I will defy the hon. member for Royal to deny this. Application forms for old age pensions were placed in the hands of the clergymen in our province by the members of their party. The clergymen were told to get them into the hands of the old people immediately, because when the election was over they were going to put old age pensions into effect.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I could take my oath to this because I was there. When the election was over, the hon. member for Royal was elected again. Then, he folded his arms again and did nothing. This is the gentleman who gets up here today and tries to make the people of this house believe that he is a champion of all pensioners in the Dominion of Canada. When he had the chance himself, and when he could have done something for the people of his own province, and as I have said many times at a time when it was needed, he folded his arms and refused to do anything for them. Now, I do not believe the people down there when they read this

statement of his that it will take more than the eloquence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to persuade old age pensioners who are condemned to live on the old age pension that they would be satisfied with an increase of $6 per month, will pay much attention to that statement. Let me add to that that in this same period of the thirties, not just old age pensioners but whole families were getting $3 per week from a Tory government and those who did not have families got 20 cents a day and were hidden back in some work camp. These are the people who stand up and say you are not going far enough. My first thought is, what would they do if they were in the driver's seat. I have given you an example of what they would do. They did nothing.
There was also a reference by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) to family allowances. This is another one which does not go too hot with the Tory party. The hon. member mentioned ten cents a day for pensions, and then he mentioned the family allowance cheque. Again, one would think, what would the Tories do if they were in the driver's seat. Well, let us go back to a conference held in Ottawa a few months ago. This is part of the record of the Progressive Conservative national convention of December 13, 1956. This is Grace Hartman of Sudbury speaking, and she said:
I notice in our social welfare section that we made no mention whatever of the family allowances and you'll remember that those were introduced by the Liberal government some years ago and they have taken the credit for them ever since. It seems to me that we. of the Conservative party, should take the initiative at this convention and offer some proposition that will increase them or improve this ruling. Sometimes we women are told that our place is in the home, we're interested in the home as well as in public life. And I would like to know just what it is we're going to be doing about these family allowances. We've covered everything else but that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the Hon. T. L. Smith, of Nova Scotia, who is the chairman of this committee to reply.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, I am very happy to say what the view of the subcommittee on this point was. We certainly did consider the question of family allowances and we felt as strongly as one can feel, or a committee can feel, that of course we are in favour of the principle of family allowances and of the continuance thereof. We felt, however, that we were not in a position to recommend now to this convention, an increase in the amount or rate at which these allowances are presently being paid. Therefore, acting on the principle that unless we were recommending something new, it would not be appropriate to suggest a recommendation or resolution to the convention, we did not include a paragraph on that particular point.
Now, that is all the interest they had in family allowances. It was not even discussed. I could read on farther, but I think my time

is rapidly disappearing and that is not necessary. In any event, they did not think the allowance could be increased.
I should like to deal with one more point that was brought up by the hon. member for Royal the other day. He mentioned the fact that today the federal government was taking practically all the tax dollar and leaving nothing for the'provinces or the municipality. I want to put a few figures on the record that I know are correct and the source from which they come is one of the most reliable.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the source?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of
Finance (Mr. Harris) and I do not believe there is a better authority in the House of Commons. On the basis of 1953-54 the percentage amount taken actually by each level of government was: federal, 71 per cent; provincial, 16 per cent; municipal, 13 per cent. This ignores the net transfers from the federal to provincial governments of $420 million in the year and the transfer by provincial governments to municipalities of $230 million. Using these corrected figures we get the following result: federal, 64 per cent, provincial 19 per cent, municipal 17 per cent.
Now, in 1939-40 the distribution was this way; federal 44 per cent, provincial 24 per cent, municipal 32 per cent. Since that time we have taken over the full payment of old age pensions, are paying family allowances -we pay all these other social services which were considered to be a provincial obligation previous to that date. Now today if we adjust those same figures taking into consideration our defence costs, we will find-I put the figures on the record: adjustments for defence, $1,250 million; veterans pensions, $250 million; debt charges, $300 million; social welfare, $800 million; federal adjusted net revenue, $1,500 million; provincial adjusted net revenue, $1,183 million; municipal adjusted net revenue, $1,041 million. When that is broken down and we take out the defence expenditures and all the services which we pay now and which were provincial obligations previous to 1939, you get these figures: federal, 40 per cent; provincial, 32 per cent and municipal 28 per cent. We are actually taking today from the taxpayer 4 per cent less than we were in 1940. However, every provincial government in this country will cry to high heaven that they are not getting their share of the taxpayer's dollar. That is what is happening in New Brunswick. All we hear down there anyway is bellyaching; that is all they know. All they can do is complain. The thing that hurts, and it hurts the people there, is the fact that in 1952 we had too much revenue and the payment was increased from $52 million to $64
The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart million. They still have not enough. If you gave them $15 million more they would still have not enough. There is a reason for it. They have got too many friends to take care of.

speechtext: What was that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said you are the last one to talk about that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What do you mean by that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What do you mean by that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
