subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what I meant, too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is exactly what I meant and I will just add, since my hon. friend interjected, that there is not a provincial project in my province on which a Liberal can get a job even if he were starving today.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a falsehood.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is correct. I know, and I can take you down there. There is no such thing around Camp Gagetown, which is a federal project. A man is not asked how he voted when he asks for work there. I would not belong to a government that did a thing like that because I am not that narrow minded. I can tell my hon. friend about a job in my own county which was a part-time job because they could only work when the tide was out. A gentleman I know well applied for work and the gentleman building the bridge said he could only give him part-time labour. He said, "Well, I will have to take it until something better comes along." Then, the man said, "You will have to drive back to St. Stephen and get a slip from Mr. Buchanan before I can put you to work." That was part-time work for four or five hours a day on a provincial government project. I can tell you that not only on that project but on the trans-Canada highway project it was a terrific problem for a Liberal to get a job.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When my hon. friend's party was in power for 17 years Conservatives could never get a job. That was the situation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman cannot tell me what happened for 17 years; I know what happened for 17 years. I am one who never believed that because a man voted against me he had to be starved to death, but that has been the attitude of the

The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart Conservative party as far back as I can remember, and my memory is good. That is the way they have been carrying on in our province. Take the Beech wood project that has been mentioned so often in this house. Who looks after the hiring and firing on the Beech wood project?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Charlotte is the only member in the house who brings cheap, untrue politics into this house, and he does it every time he speaks.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In reply to that I say to the hon. member for Royal that he thinks he can use everything he likes in this house and I should not reply to him, but I can tell him that as long as I am here- I do not know how long that will be-I am going to reply to him. I have replied to remarks in connection with old age pensions. I ask the hon. member whether he can rise in his place and deny what I said about old age pensions?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I can, and I deny it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have lived in that province and I know that we went through a period when old age pensions were paid and we did not get a single dollar. There is a little more to it than that. During the seven or eight years that I have spoken of we of New Brunswick paid our proportionate part of federal taxation to take care of the other provinces. The excuse given by the leader of the Tory party in the 1935 election, and he was defeated as a result of this, was that we did not have the money to pay old age pensions. But I can tell the hon. member this. After the Liberals came into power they found the money to pay the old age pensions and they put it into circulation. They took the bill the Tories had hidden away in some pigeonhole; they dusted it off and put it into execution, and they got pensions within 10 months of the time the Liberal government took over. I will tell the hon. member for Royal that the day will come-and it is not too far distant,-when they will take over again, because it will take the people only a short time to realize that some housecleaning ought to be done. When you have one-third of the population on the payroll of the provincial government it is time to do something about it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There will be a housecleaning in my hon. friend's constituency the next time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That might happen.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will happen.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am very doubtful that it will happen. I still have faith in the people of Charlotte. I do not believe they


want a Tory to represent them. I am going back to Charlotte with every expectation of being elected again.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You will be terribly
disappointed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I referred a few minutes ago to the project at Beech wood. The gentleman who does the hiring and firing at Beechwood was the provincial Tory member for about 25 or 28 years. Well, there was a time a few years back when those who were in the potato-growing industry were in a very bad way. It was decided that there would be several carloads of potatoes shipped away. They were to be subsidized, given away, or something, and the potato growers were to get a few dollars. The gentleman who has charge of the hiring and firing at Beechwood today let it be known publicly that no Liberal growing potatoes could receive a single nickel. The only policy he had was to give to his Conservative friends. That is the gentleman who is doing the hiring and firing at Beechwood today. If my hon. friend from Royal would like to see them, I can show him letters from Liberals living within a stone's throw of Beechwood who have never been able to get on the payroll and who will never be able to get on the payroll as long as we have a Tory government in New Brunswick, because they will look after their friends. If you do not vote as they vote you can starve as far as they are concerned.
I am going to resume my seat, but I wish to repeat: if the hon. member from New Brunswick, the Conservative hon. member, thinks he can rise in his place in this house and condemn the government with which I am associated without my making some reply, then he has the wrong fellow to deal with. I do not intend this government to be abused when I believe it is right. I have felt it was right from the day I first came here and I shall continue thinking that way until something happens that will change my views. But I intend to support the government; I intend to stand on my feet and condemn any of the propaganda that they bring into the House of Commons.

speechtext: I cannot tell the hon. gentleman that because I am not the Minister of Public Works, but I will tell him this. I know of many who are working in the House of Commons who do not support the Liberal government; that is as far as I am concerned.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last two speakers have used their time in this debate to cover practically any subject they wished. Under those conditions I am going to deal with a subject that I am very interested in, since my constituents are worried about it at the present time. I refer to the fruit industry. I feel the federal government has a direct responsibility to the industry because in the 1930's, when the industry started to build up in Canada, the fruit-growers received government protection and encouragement. I would draw to the attention of the government the fact that this was included in the horticultural council's presentation made to the government within the last month or so. I would like to quote it:
The protection extended to the fruit and vegetable producers in the early thirties provided the incentive for expansion of production in Canada; an abundance of supply resulted in very reasonable price levels for Canadian consumers. The extent to which that protection against "dumping" has been whittled away, and the Canadian producer left exposed is the cause of the alarm today among Canadian producers, and prompts this "request for action".
It is this question of unfair competition, or so-called dumping, that still plays havoc with our industry that I should like to deal with, particularly in connection with soft fruits and vegetables. The government's present policy, and its definition of dumping, have proved useless in stopping the practice. Actually, it continues to increase, much to the detriment of our producers each year. Early this year the British Columbia fruit growers association passed the following resolution covering the same point, and with your permission, sir, I should like to quote from it:
Whereas heavy crop years in soft fruits occur simultaneously in the western United States and British Columbia, and
Whereas experience has shown that in such years American soft fruit surpluses are dumped indiscriminately on the Canadian market, thus completely disrupting and demoralizing the orderly marketing of the British Columbia crop, and
Whereas provision to prevent such dumping is made in the general agreement on tariffs and trade yet, because of the inadequately defined antidumping clause, enforcement is practically impossible :
The Budget-Mr. Jones
Therefore be it resolved by this 1957 B.C.F.G.A. convention that the executive be requested to petition immediately the federal government to have the anti-dumping clause of the general agreement on trade and tariffs rewritten and clarified so that the "prevailing price" in the country of origin may not be the price prevailing in any isolated local market but must be the average price prevailing in at least six principal markets in the country of origin.
Last year I suggested that dumping could be defined by accepting the Canadian cost of production as a yardstick and any importation at a price below that should be regarded as dumping.
In view of the unanimity shown by the whole organized fruit industry as displayed through their briefs and resolutions which have already been presented to the federal government, I trust the minister will take steps immediately to carry out their very reasonable requests.
I would like now to quote from the brief of the horticultural council. They say:
The nature or form of the competition to which our producers object most strenuously is imports at "distress" prices at the peak or clean-up of American harvesting which frequently collides with the commencement of Canadian harvesting. Under these conditions the American producer may have received a premium price, or at least a good average price on a large proportion of his crop, but his "clean-up" sales can set the market price for a very large proportion of the Canada crop of the same commodity, and prevent any possibility of the Canadian producer selling any portion of his crop at premium prices, or even benefiting to a normal extent from a short-crop condition that might exist in Canada.
No one can convince the farmer of the fairness or equity of a trade agreement which makes no realistic provision to protect a primary producer against this type of imports.
I am not going to take a great deal of time in dealing with this problem because I have already mentioned it and I think the minister is aware of the serious plight of farmers not only in British Columbia but in other parts of Canada through this unfair and unjust competition which is growing by leaps and bounds.
I would ask the minister to remember that at one time this industry flourished under the protection of the government and if they have the same interest now as they did then they should grant the industry the same protection which they accorded it in the past.
In line with my personal thoughts I would also suggest to the minister that a great deal could be done to protect the industry by setting up a board to provide for the orderly importing of fruit and vegetables, for instance through export-import boards, and the setting of appropriate quotas which will first enable the Canadian fruit and vegetable industry to plan for the future which they cannot do today; second, guarantee Canadian

The Budget-Mr. Jones consumers an economical supply of good quality fruit and vegetables at fair prices; and third, provide security for the fruit and vegetable farmers and workers in the industry. This will also ensure fair trades practices and prohibit the unfair dumping of fruit and vegetables into Canada at distressed prices.
I will conclude my remarks concerning dumping by asking the minister to read again the briefs presented by the two main bodies representing fruit farmers in Canada so that he can appreciate the extent of the damage that is being done to that industry.
The convention recently held in Penticton to which I referred earlier also asked for a price support for the fruit industry such as is already given to some sections of our agricultural industry including meat and poultry. I also mentioned their request for minimum support for the current year of at least 25 cents a box on fruit. I trust the government will give consideration to this request for immediate assistance. This industry is ailing but is not beyond recovery if the federal government will apply the necessary remedies. A floor price would be one valuable remedy which the government could apply to give a measure of stability and security to the growers.
Another resolution passed at the convention called for the extension of unemployment insurance benefits to farm workers and particularly orchard workers. I understand that this matter has been given consideration by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) during the last year or two. Surely the department has found some solution to what appears to be a minor problem of administration. The benefits of this act at the present time are being denied to approximately 100,000 of our primary producers in Canada. I would ask the Minister of Labour to hasten the bringing in of necessary changes in the act in order to extend unemployment insurance benefits to a very essential group in our economy.
I would like now to request the Minister of Agriculture to extend the research work that is presently being carried out in our industry. I appreciate the splendid work that is being done at the present time but I feel that a great deal more could be done with by-products if adequate funds and suitable buildings and equipment were provided. In addition to research into byproducts research could be conducted in relation to marketing, packing and shipping.
I am pleased that at the present time there is a team composed of officers of the Department of Agriculture and members of

our industry who are carrying out research into packing, marketing and shipping in New Zealand and Australia. I hope that when they return with useful recommendations the government will adopt them.
Agriculture in general and those I represent seek just one thing, economic equality with labour and industry or, in other words, a fair share of our national wealth. While Canada as a whole is enjoying general prosperity I would point out that the benefits of this prosperity have not descended equally on all sections of Canada and especially those areas depending entirely on agriculture with the result that many of our smaller communities find it difficult to carry on with the necessary improvements.
I have in mind one such community that is faced with the urgent need to replace its entire irrigation system. For that purpose it has to borrow approximately $270,000 and must find this money on the open market probably at a very high rate of interest because it is a depressed area owing to loss through frost and other conditions that brought depression into the immediate neighbourhood. Failing this the community will have to abandon the whole plan which in this case would mean the ruination of the entire fruit industry in that particular area.
I contend that the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act should be reopened to take care of such areas as the one to which I have just referred. It is true, we might be told, that this act which made money available at 2 per cent for self-liquidating projects was designed to assist municipalities by making capital available at cheap interest during a period of crisis, but may I point out to the minister that a crisis exists today in some of our agricultural communities such as the one I mentioned.
I feel this act was a good one and if it was ever needed in Canada it is needed today to assist municipalities to cope with the increasing need for the building of necessary self-liquidating projects to take care of the natural growth of population and the influx of immigrants.
If the government is willing to reactivate this act to cover the whole of Canada much good could result. Failing that would it not be possible to reopen it as far as the distressed areas are concerned or, if it is the wish of the government, on a regional basis?
I know that after it was generally closed some years ago it was reopened in favour of Quebec when it had ceased to operate in other parts of Canada, and if an exception could be made in favour of Quebec at that time the same principle could apply to these distressed areas now.

I feel that the tight money policy which is now in effect has placed many municipalities in an impossible situation. The growing need for public works and the current cost of borrowing money has caused them to abandon many urgently necessary projects and this situation obtains right across Canada. The reopening of this act would be their salvation and would allow them to play their full role in supplying utilities in the fast growing urban areas.
I would now like to say a word or two on behalf of three groups who I am satisfied did not receive fair treatment in the budget. I refer to blind pensioners, widows of veterans and single veterans in receipt of war veterans allowance. I urge the minister to reconsider these three groups to see if something cannot be done to raise their standards of living to compare with those standards that have been raised slightly. I know from experience that it is almost impossible for a single veteran to maintain decent surroundings or a decent home and provide the necessary food, clothing and shelter on $60 a month. I urge the minister to reconsider the decision he came to with regard to these three groups because what I say about the veterans applies also to the blind pensioners and the widows of war veterans.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to compliment the Minister of Finance upon his presentation of a budget which is a great tribute to the wisdom and farsightedness of this administration in that the principal problem of the minister has been to plan his fiscal year on the basis of another financial surplus.
Members of the official opposition may criticize the government and the Minister of Finance as they wish, but they must admit that in their own party record they have never found themselves in such an enviable position. Under the Liberal administration and under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) Canada has enjoyed a period of unparalleled prosperity and has at the same time been able to offer more to the citizens of Canada than at any other time in history.
Under the budget we have just received, more than a hundred and fifty thousand Canadians receive additional benefits. Those who decry the prosperity budget certainly do not include those who will be receiving increased old age pensions or increased family allowances. Neither will they include those who are now relieved by a further tax exemption from paying any income taxes, even though they receive the benefits referred to.
The Budget-Mr. Bourque
The disappointed ones are those who are already receiving record incomes and are enjoying to the utmost the second highest living standard in the world. As they drive their cars, own their own homes, look at television and enjoy all the other fine products of modern life, they complain that there is little in the budget for them. They do not need any help. They are doing very well as it is. The minister has instead shown concern for those in need and his budget is designed to help them. For those who think in terms of all the people there is little fault to be found with this budget.
And now may I ask the indulgence of this house for a short while so that I may bring to the attention of hon. members something which I believe is of concern to all Canadians. Several months ago a magazine published in the United States printed an article which seriously slandered the French-Canadian people. Widely distributed in Canada, this article is one which could cause disunity in this country. It is, of course, the right of an editor to exercise his own judgment in what he publishes. But it is not the right of an editor to create dissension and then refuse to permit the other side of the story to be told. Immediately upon reading the offensive article in Esquire magazine I wrote the publisher. I received from him a non-committal answer. I wrote the publisher again and in reply to this letter received the same reply that I had received to my first communication.
We in Canada believe in freedom of the press. But we believe that along with this freedom there must be a sense of responsibility. I believe that the editors of Esquire delight in causing trouble and dissension in this country. They show no sense of responsibility and are not entitled to any consideration on our part.
I wish this statement to go on the record and I wish to read my correspondence with Esquire to go along with it. If these irresponsible editors can distribute in our country their disreputable attacks on one group of our citizens, they can as well attack another group tomorrow. We have iri Canada a serious struggling group of honest magazines. They are swamped by the overruns of a lot of cheap trash published below the border. We go a long way when we allow this trash to circulate here at all; surely we do not have to admit trash which also consists of slanderous attacks on our own people. The letter which I addressed to

The Budget-Mr. Bourque the editors of Esquire under date of December 24, 1956 was as follows:
Gentlemen.
Since your publication came into existence I have been one of your constant readers and for many years have very much enjoyed reading it.
I was somewhat shocked by the statements made in an article published in your January 1957 issue entitled "The Shooting of Alanna Boole" by Gerald Kersh.
I would appreciate if you would publish the attached letter in your next issue of Esquire.
Thank you in anticipation of this favour, I remain.
Sincerely yours,
Romuald Bourque, M.P. Mayor, City of Outremont, Province of Quebec, Canada.
The attached letter, also dated December 24, 1956, reads as follows:
To the Editors of Esquire.
Dear Sirs:
Your many good friends in Canada were shocked and, I am afraid, angered by some of the statements made in the article "The Shooting of Alanna Boole" by Gerald Kersh. They were shocked because they have never found Esquire to be unfair or deliberately inaccurate: and they were angered because there were so many indications of personal prejudice in the author's biased portrait of French Canadians.
Editors can be misled and when they are, I believe it the duty of those who are aggrieved to seek to inform them. As a member of the Canadian parliament, representing a constituency which is both French and English speaking, and as mayor of the city of Outremont which is also a bilingual community, I wish not to protest against an article which was undoubtedly published in good faith, but rather to correct some of the glaring errors in fact and interpretation. I think that you as editors and publishers would wish to be correctly informed, and I think that your readers, particularly those in the United States, have a right to be given a truer picture of their northern neighbours.
It is always difficult for an individual brought up in one language and one culture to judge fairly people who speak a different tongue and have a different cultural background. People of French extraction are prone to look down upon those whose ancestry is Anglo Saxon and to find their manners and customs just as peculiar as their own manners and customs appear to the English. However, when any such individual takes the time and makes the effort to study the culture of others, he soon finds that in every national group there are virtues and qualities that command admiration and respect. This is as true of French-Canadians as it is of any other people anywhere.
To say that the French-Canadian is without culture or good manners is to slander a people who are recognized by their English-speaking compatriots as the main contributors to the culture of Canada. This young country which is notably lacking in many of the old world's cultural attributes has a recognized French-Canadian literature which commands respect in France as well as among educated people in many foreign countries. The leading English critics consistently point to French Canada's group of contemporary novelists and playwrights as the freshest, most invigorating writers in North America today.
Esquire itself, might do worse than commission some articles from Roger Lemelin, Gabrielle Roy or any one of a number of modern French creative

writers. They, and others, have much to say, and they say it in a manner which is both cultured and exciting.
In the field of fine art. French Canada's talented and lively school of expressionists has a wide audience in France as. well as here at home. Its traditionalists are represented in many foreign galleries. The French Canadian is daring in expression and highly skilled in the use of colour.
French Canada has also established an unique record in television drama, a new art form with which even the greatest United States producers and actors are not always entirely successful.
Participation of French Canadian actors in the Stratford Shakespearean Festival opened the eyes of many United States visitors and English speaking Canadians to the French Canadian stage which is a vital, living force in Quebec province.
To say that French Canadians have made no contributions to music is, of course, a statement that can only be founded upon ignorance. Many French Canadians have won world reputations in music; a Pelletier was for many years conductor at the Metropolitan Opera; Calixa Lavallee, the composer of "O Canada", was known as the Father of American Music; L'Heure de Concert, produced in Montreal, is one of the great music programs of North American television today.
No number of words can, of course, portray a people's culture to another. Such a culture is a discovery each one must make for himself. Every year, friendly people from the United States come to visit French Canada by the thousands. They, I am sure, take back an entirely different picture of their hosts than the one that has been presented to them in Esquire. They find here a friendly, hospitable people, rich in tradition, gay in manner, fond of good music, good and stimulating conversation. They will not find here an Old France or a European province, but a North American France, speaking and honouring the same French language but adapting to it, as do all people of all languages, the idioms and the nuances of their region and their surroundings.
The culture of French Canada is here for all time. It is traditional, it is true but above all it is a living culture and not one to be despised or belittled by those who do not share it.
As a French Canadian, proud of my heritage. I have learned to appreciate and understand the traditions and culture of the United States. I can distinguish between, but do not discriminate against, the culture of New England and that of the Middle West. With my fellow Canadians, whether English or French, I seek not uncritical praise but rather understanding. And that, I am sure, would be the wish also of the editors of Esquire.
Yours very truly,
Romuald Bourque, M.P.
Mayor of the City of Outremont,
Province of Quebec, Canada.
I received the following letter dated January 8, 1957. It was a circular letter, to which had been added my name:
Dear Mr. Bourque:
Thank you for your comments on "The Shooting of Alanna Boole," by Gerald Kersh, which appeared in the January issue of Esquire. We always appreciate a word from readers, even if it is a chiding one.
In reply, but not necessarily in retort, permit me to say that since Esquire is not a magazine of opinion-that is, it contains the comments of contributors but does not guide or direct their points of view-this often leaves quite a bit of latitude on the part of the author. We judge an article on its

merits, for style or interest or other content: but in this case of a distinguished writer such as Gerald Kersh, who is certainly qualified to speak for himself, we would not alter his point of view within certain limits of taste even if we were to disagree with it. We are, therefore, pleased to pass along your reactions to author Kersh, who will also be obliged to you for your courtesies.
Meanwhile, with only a passing glance at the many complimentary articles we have published about Quebec over the years, I hope that your pleasure in the Quebec report by Richard Joseph, to appear in our forthcoming May issue, will more than compensate for your disappointment in the present opus.
Sincerely,
Frederic A. Birmingham.
And to this I replied on January 22, 1957:
Dear Sir,
Your letter of January 8, 1957, intimates that you are not willing to permit those who do not agree with Gerald Kersh's estimate of French Canadians to answer his insulting and unreasonable charges. Your attitude surprises me since I have always believed that you, as all other responsible editors, believed that freedom of expression extended to those who are attacked as well as those who are the attackers.
The views expressed by Mr. Kersh are obviously his own and not those of Esciuire. However, since you made space available to him to air those views, and presumably paid him well for doing so, it seems only fair that those whom he attacks should be allowed to respond, particularly when they do not ask to be paid for so doing.
No writer, however talented, should expect to have all his statements go unchallenged. In the case of Mr. Kersh, who seems to be unknown in this country, the right to reply is even greater because he obviously writes from prejudice rather than experience and appears to me to be a completely irresponsible individual.
In Canada, there are approximately four million Canadians who are French speaking. In the United States, I believe, there are more than two million people who still look upon French Canada as home. It is surely not a policy of Esquire to deliberately insult these people and deny them the right of rebuttal.
Your rights as an editor are not disputed. You obviously have control over everything that appears in your publication. But your readers have some rights, too. These include the right to hear both sides of the story. The fact that you are publishing an article on Quebec in a later issue does not constitute an answer to the charges made by Mr. Kersh.
The policy of the Canadian government is one which favours the exchange of ideas between nations. No tariffs are imposed upon United States or any other foreign magazines entering this country. We favour the free exchange of views. But when the free exchange, which means proper representation for both sides, is denied by a publisher himself, then the time has come when the desirability of unhindered distribution of that publisher's magazine in this country may be seriously questioned.
Your respect for your French Canadian readers is obviously very slight; your refusal to permit these readers to defend themselves against unprovoked insult is indefensible.
Sincerely yours,
Romuald Bourque, M.P.
Mayor of the City of Outremont.
I received a reply to that on January 24,
1957-the same letter that they had already
The Budget-Mr. Bourque sent me-the circular letter they had sent me on January 8. To this I wrote my final letter dated February 12, 1957.
Dear Mr. Birmingham:
Surely, the courtesy of an intelligent reply is not too much to expect from an editor or publisher. The same form letter received in response to two personally written letters of protest cannot be considered either as good manners or good public relations for a publishing company such as yours.
In good faith and with goodwill, I took the time to write you last December regarding what I considered to be unfair and unjustified comments on one-third of the Canadian people published in Esquire last fall. I believed that as responsible editors, you would wish to provide space in your letters column to a reasonable presentation of the other side of the story. Apparently, I was mistaken. On January 8, 1957, I received a curt reply indicating that my views were of no interest.
Because I still believed that no editor would willingly be placed in a position of refusing a rebuttal to a prejudiced article, I wrote to you again, and on January 24 I received a copy of the same form letter I had previously received. This may simply indicate that you do not read your mail, or it may be that you do not have any interest in reader reaction to what you publish. '
Strangely, I along with many other Canadians, am just this week in receipt of another form letter from your company, this time urging us to become subscribers to Esquire. Surely, you insult our intelligence.
In Canada, as in the United States, we have long enjoyed a tradition of freedom of the press. This privilege however, is one which should be deserved and which should not be abused. Any publication which seeks to divide one section of the Canadian public against another or which seeks to hold up to scorn and ridicule a third of our population, no longer deserves the right of unhindered distribution through the Canadian mails.
Many foreign publications circulate freely in Canada, entering this country without duty and free of any Canadian taxation. They are admitted because they add to the exchange of information between countries and contribute to our knowledge and culture. A few publications are banned from entry either because they are politically subversive or because they are immoral and indecent in character. Publications which deliberately seek to create dissension in Canada could come within either of these classifications.
To the troubled world which exists today, the United States is seeking to provide enlightened leadership. Millions of your dollars are being spent to promote understanding and friendship in Asia and other parts of the world. Next door, the United States has a neighbour whose friendship does not need to be bought but whose friendship can be imperilled by reckless and irresponsible treatment by editors of magazines which circulate in this country. We cherish our good relations with the United States too greatly to permit them to be endangered by such irresponsible editors
The growing antagonism to the United States resulting from attitudes and opinions expressed in some United States magazines is a matter which is already causing concern here and which has reached the attention of your president.
I would ask the courtesy of a reply and the assurance that you will publish my first letter and that you do not intend to continue publication of unfair and thoroughly prejudiced attacks upon mv countrymen.	'
Sincerely,
Romuald Bourque, M.P.
Mayor, City of Outremont,
Province of Quebec, Canada,

The Budget-Mr. Hees
And to this I received a final answer from Esquire on February 8, 1957.
It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Bourque:
Thank you for your recent letter and for your interest in Esquire magazine. We found your comments most interesting and appreciate your taking time to express your reaction to the magazine's content.
Unfortunately, we are able to print only a very few of the many letters received; however, time and space restrictions permitting, we will publish your letter in a future issue of Esquire.
Please feel free to write again, telling us your views of Esquire.
Cordially,
Esquire, Inc.
A. T. McIntyre Sound and Fury

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the call from the other place came a few minutes before six o'clock I was saying that in the five years between 1948 and 1953 foreign investors contributed two-thirds of the additional capital supplied to our oil and gas industry, more than two-thirds of the additional capital supplied to our mining and smelting industry, and just over half of the additional capital supplied to our manufacturing industries. The indications are that this process has increased during the past three years.
Government spokesmen try to explain this situation away by claiming that Canada is merely going through the same process which the United States passed through at the height of its development period. Figures prove this contention to be completely untrue.
The year 1914 was the peak year for foreign investments in the United States compared to its national income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What year?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1914. At that time the United States had a population of 94 millions, a national income of $45 billion and foreign-owned assets in the country totalled $7.5 billion, or 15 per cent of the national income.
Today in Canada we have a population of 16 millions, a national income of approximately $23 billion and foreign-owned assets in this country amount to $15 billion or 65 per cent of our national income. On a per capita basis, foreign owned assets in the United States in 1941 amounted to about $75 per person. In Canada the per capita figure for 1953 was $790, for 1954 it was $822, for 1955 it was $860 and it is $940 today. And so we see, Mr. Speaker, there is no similarity between the situation which existed in the United States at the time when its foreign investment compared to its national income was at its height and the situation in Canada today.
The United States retained control of its development and we are losing more and more of ours as each year goes by. I believe that to be losing control of our industry and natural resources is a very serious situation to be faced by a young and growing country such as ours. The question is, of course, what are we going to do about it?
I believe that what we must do is to work out a program by which we will do a great deal more of our own developing than we have done in recent years and thereby retain a far greater control of our industries and resources than we do today.
The next question, of course, is how is this going to be done? I believe it can be done by taking five constructive steps. The first is to revise our taxation system so that

The Budget-Mr. Hees
the incentives which are made available to Canadian development companies will be at least as favourable as those provided by the United States government to American companies investing in Canada.
One example of how the government is making it difficult for Canadians to compete for ownership and control of their natural resources is in the oil and gas industry. The United States government allows an American company to write off the entire bonus price paid for the drilling rights on an oil reservation. The Canadian government permits no write-off whatever. This enables United States companies to outbid Canadian firms because they know they will be allowed to write off the entire bonus price which they have paid if the area proves to be non-productive.
Another example of how the Canadian government is discriminating against Canadian oil and gas companies is in the matter of depletion allowances. The United States government allows depletion allowances of 274 per cent of gross income to the limit of 50 per cent of the net income. The Canadian government merely allows a depletion allowance of 33J per cent of the net. The more generous depletion allowances which the United States companies receive puts them in a far better position to carry on exploration and development than Canadian companies and that is the main reason why they have done so much more of this work than we have.
Another example of how the Canadian government places Canadian industry in a less favourable position is in the matter of research. In Great Britain and the United States all expenditures for research are allowed as tax write-offs whether they be capital expenditures or current expenditures. In Canada the government merely allows a write-off of 5 per cent of the taxable income of the previous year unless the minister makes some special concession and even then of course the company must wait anywhere from six to nine months before they know what the minister's decision will be.
Research is needed most after a bad year or when a company is just starting to operate and that of course is the time when taxable income is at its very lowest. This simply points up the unreality of the government's approach to this whole problem.
The second step which I suggest the government should take is to create by budgetary measures an economic atmosphere in this country which will induce new industries to start up and present industries to expand.
One such measure would be the introduction of a graduated corporation tax which

would apply to new industries and would be spread over the period it is estimated that a new industry would require to get on its feet.
Another suggestion would be a graduated corporation tax on protfis between, let us say, $20,000 a year and $50,000. At the present time a company pays 20 per cent tax on profits up to $20,000 a year and then on the next $1,000 of profit it pays the full tax of 47 per cent. This provides very little if any incentive to a small company to branch out into the sphere where it could be considered a medium sized or big business with all the additional requirements and headaches this implies.
Still another suggestion would be the granting of accelerated depreciation on plants and equipment to a new company so that it would be enabled to write off its investment more quickly and induce those who might be thinking of going into such an enterprise to more readily embark upon it.
The third constructive step which I suggest is that we should create a national industrial development board which would work with the provinces, municipalities and transportation companies to obtain maximum concessions for potential industries, and by advertising these concessions make Canadian businessmen aware of the opportunities that are awaiting development.
The fourth step I suggest would be to provide an incentive to United States companies who are developing Canada to increase the proportion of their stock which would be owned by Canadians by offering tax concessions in proportions to the percentage of stock held by Canadians.
The fifth step I suggest is that we create in the mind of the average investor a preference for sound development enterprises over investment in bonds. I believe this could be done through films, by speeches by leading statesmen, by editorials in our leading newspapers, and by literature put out by our financial houses to advise businessmen and Canadians of the great opportunities which exist for investment in the development of this country.
In conclusion, I believe that if we will take these steps we can finance the great industrial development of which this country is capable and at the same time retain control of that development here in Canada. United States and foreign capital is of course most welcome but it is one thing to invite investment in our country and another to allow outsiders to take over the economic control of it. I believe it is up to us to see to it that by our vision, initiative and courage we retain control of the future development of our own country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some disappointments in this budget for some of us, but in the main I am sure it will be accepted by a large majority of the house and, it follows, by a large majority of the people of Canada. I intend of course to support the budget when the vote is taken and to vote against the amendment which will be before us later this day. There are some things in the budget which are of great interest to British Columbia, and also in the estimates which have been before the house for some time, but I think one of the most important announcements of government policy that has been made in many years in so far as British Columbia is concerned is the announcement of new policy in connection with the development of power in British Columbia, more specifically in the Columbia basin.
The announcement made in Vancouver the other day by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) will I am sure be met with enthusiasm and great joy in all parts of British Columbia, and particularly in the southern mainland which faces a power shortage within the next few years, and in both Kootenay East and Kootenay West which comprise an area which in all probability will become the industrial empire of America as a result of this development. There is no reason why our industrial expansion should not match that of the north of the United States Northwest Pacific area where because of the power made available by the construction of the Grand Coulee and other dams, the production is worth something like $10 billion annually. We should be able to match that production when the vast power potentials of the Canadian Columbia have been developed.
Another important aspect of this announcement is that it will put an end forever to the offers and rumours of offers from power interests in the United States to come to Canada to build dams and weirs for the purpose of controlling the water flow for their own use. Certainly the Kaiser deal will be as dead as a mackerel. As you know, that deal was effectively stunned by the International River Improvements Act which was passed in 1955.
The announcement of this policy should advance the completion of the Mica creek project by at least six years. We realize that no single administration or no single enterprise could raise the money necessary to build this huge dam which in all probability will cost close to half a billion dollars when all the installations and equipment are considered. An offer has been made to the province of British Columbia under which
The Budget-Mr. Byrne the government of Canada is prepared to sit down with them to discuss this matter at their pleasure. It is certainly something for which we are truly thankful and I am sure the province generally shares my enthusiasm.
This offer should also expedite the negotiations which are to take place in May between the Canadian government and the United States authorities with respect to the downstream benefits on the Columbia and Kootenay rivers. For that reason the building of the Libby dam should be brought nearer to reality. The building of the Libby dam will bring about great improvements in my riding as it will have the effect of controlling the floods on the Kootenay flats and thus enhancing the value of much of that property to a great extent. It would open up the flats to use by smaller farms and the growing of wheat, which is not profitable on that type of land, could be discontinued and other types of produce grown which would bring in higher returns per acre.
There are other matters in which the federal government will participate to a large extent in British Columbia, more particularly in Kootenay East, and I refer to the activities of the national parks branch which is also under the energetic direction of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage).
This is in the Kootenay, Yoho Park and, of course, the adjacent parks of Banff and Jasper which are just across the border in Alberta and he will have spent $10 million on roads and other construction. I believe that on trunk roads alone they will have spent about $7 million by the end of 1957. The trans-Canada highway passes through two of these national parks, the Banff national park and the Yoho national park, and in the construction of the trans-Canada highway, which is entirely a federal responsibility in the national parks, a further $11 million will be expended. This means, I understand, that by next year the highway from Banff through to Kamloops will have been virtually completed up to trans-Canada standards, with hard surface.
The federal government has offered within the past year to incur considerable expenditure on the Golden to Revelstoke section of the trans-Canada highway. I understand that an agreement has been reached with the provincial government to apply the 90 per cent formula to the cost of the trans-Canada in this section. It is, indeed, a very costly section of the highway; snow sheds, tunnels and so forth will be required, and we are very grateful that in the not too distant future we shall have a highway on

The Budget-Mr. Byrne which we can travel directly to Vancouver from the riding of East Kootenay.
Now I am going to make a suggestion for further expenditure by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and this expenditure will, of course, be requested specifically for the riding of East Kootenay. Not because it is the riding of East Kootenay but because a section of the highway leading to the four national parks that I have just mentioned is a highway upon which there is converging traffic from all the midwestern states of the United States and the western United States.
One of these highways is known as highway 93. It stretches from the heart of Mexico to Alaska, and when the provincial government has completed a short section of the highway that is known as Elco cutoff between Elco and Roosevelt there will be sufficient highway leading to these parks, and as I have said, a highway going directly from Mexico to Alaska. A lot of traffic will go through there.
The other converging highway leads from Kingsgate, the second largest port of entry in British Columbia and joins the northbound highway at Cranbrook, and the traffic during the summer is almost unbelievable. The section I have in mind reaches from 13 miles north of Kimberley to Radium. I would suggest that inasmuch as this is an access highway road to these four national parks and since it is certainly not in such a condition that it is capable of handling the traffic that it is bearing, and will have to bear, the federal government should take into consideration building this highway on a 50-50 basis with the province of British Columbia.
We were indeed grateful for an announcement that was made some weeks ago that the federal government is prepared to assist in the building of a highway parallel to the Alaska panhandle, and open up the rich mineral and forest resources of northern British Columbia.
The premier of British Columbia, when advised of the announcement by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) recently, was sceptical of the offer regarding the power project, and said he would prefer to speak to the Prime Minister. He obviously does not realize that the cabinet in Ottawa does not operate as a "one man show" as they do in British Columbia, but that each and every minister, when he makes an announcement is speaking for the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and for the entire cabinet. The premier made the observation that he was not concerned about speaking with the travelling Minister of Fisheries. Undoubtedly


the Minister of Fisheries does get around, and gets things done. He is a very capable minister doing a good job for British Columbia as is the Minister of National Defence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like now to say a few words about the old age security program.

speechtext: A poor program.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear someone say it is a poor program, but in my opinion it is the best program in existence in the world today. It is not a welfare program, as many would have us believe. The welfare aspect of old age pensions was left to the provincial governments at their own requests when the British North America Act was revised for the purpose of bringing in old age security, and this is the section dealing with these representations.
94 (a) It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but any law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions will not affect the operation of any law, present or future, of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
I have taken the trouble, Mr. Speaker, to go to the library and get some of the reports of the various provinces on their welfare programs and 1 have done some study of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures which appear in the Canada Year Book. Old age security provisions have resulted in a much lower welfare cost to the provinces, and that is the statement which I intend to prove here this evening.
Before dealing with the province of British Columbia, I will give the national picture. As far as old age pensions are concerned in 1951 there were 300,000 persons receiving

old age pensions at a cost to the federal government of about $100 million and a related cost to the provinces which, as you know, were on a cost sharing basis. The number receiving federal old age security in 1956 was nearly 900,000, at a cost to the federal treasury of almost $400 million.

In 1956 the provincial government paid $5,425,714 to recipients of old age security and old age assistance. I believe that was prior to the $5 increase in the supplement but nevertheless that was in 1956. The federal government paid $125 million more to the recipients of old age pensions in Ontario than did the province of Ontario.
Now, there was a little matter brought to my attention this morning, an article in the Globe and Mail-I do not read it often-in which welfare minister Cecile of the province of Ontario had this to say:
Welfare Minister Cecile yesterday expressed doubt that all the funds collected by the federal government for old age security pensions is actually used for that purpose.
Well, I think that is reflection on the intelligence of all the members of this house. We know that for three years there had to be payments of between $40 million and $50 million from the treasury to make up the difference between the taxes which were set aside for that purpose and the actual payments themselves.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Be fair, even to a Tory, and read the rest of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then, the minister went on to say that our old age security program appeared to be inferior to that of the United States. I have told you something of our old age security program, and I am going to outline in a few words the old age and survivors insurance of the United States. I find that 85 per cent to 90 per cent of all the wage and salary earners and self-employed persons are covered under this insurance. The most of the state and municipal employees are not covered, and there is a large percentage of farm labour that is not eligible. The average benefits are a little higher for single persons. The average benefit for a single person under that scheme is $62 per month. Of course, if he is still employed or has any earnings of any appreciable amount, he cannot receive it. There is a means test, whereas under the old age security program one receives the $46 when he reaches 70

without qualification. If the man is married, his wife also receives $46, making a total of $92. The married recipient in the United States receives $65 and his wife, upon reaching the age of 65 receives half of his payment. If he has any income or is still employed, he does not receive the pension. I have pointed out that a Canadian, under the same circumstances, may receive $92 at the age of 70, and his income is not questioned. Old age security is on a universal basis and no one is barred. This fact must be taken into account when the government considers increases in old age security payments.
It should be recalled, as I pointed out, that in British Columbia the supplement is $20 per month so that a man and his wife may receive up to $120 in that province. Now, that is as good as anything that the United States has. I make no apology for that. The state of California may have something better, I do not know.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the state of Oregon and the state of Washington.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the United States a participant pays into this fund at the rate of 2J per cent of his wages up to $4,200 so that that would mean a maximum of $90.50 whereas under our old age security program the maximum is $60. An employer pays the equivalent amount, a maximum up to $90.50. If a person is self-employed, such as doctors, lawyers and so on, he pays up to $135. There is another feature about the United States plan and that is for the first five years no one received anything after the plan was instituted. After 15 years of operation the maximum being received was $23. I think it is generally understood in this house that when the principle of old age security came under discussion, we could not possibly make it on a contributory basis, otherwise there would have been this long waiting period before anyone would have been covered. We took care of all those who had made some savings for old age, and the $40 made up for the depreciation of the dollar. In this way, their old age was in a measure secured.
In the United States there was a waiting period so, all in all, when we are considering the statement made by Mr. Cecile, I think we can say that it was made without proper study of our system. Of course, I understand that he is new in the job and he does not have the same understanding of the situation as his predecessor had. His predecessor came to Ottawa and agreed in every respect with what was being done in the way of old age security. That is all I have to say.
28, 1957
The Budget-Mr. Patterson

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sure the minister should be aware by this time that the budget which he brought down on March 14 has failed to receive the endorsation of the people across the country. Following what has become recognized as Liberal policy, the minister bluntly states that we can expect no concessions so far as income tax reductions are concerned. Then he goes on to exhort the people of Canada to spend less and save more, in other words, lest the little bit that is left after they pay their taxes should plunge our whole economy into the dark seas of inflation. I think the minister should realize that all that the great majority have left after they pay their taxes would not have too much effect so far as inflationary tendencies are concerned. I would think his exhortation sounds a little out of order and a little ridiculous when we consider all the factors which are involved.
We are all aware, of course, of the high rates of taxation and the burden of taxation that are resting upon the people of this country. I believe that one man who recognizes this most clearly is the Minister of Finance himself, because I remember his first year as Minister of Finance when he was quoted in the press as having said that the people of Canada were labouring under a very heavy load of taxation. I believe he stated at that time that he was amazed at the patience with which they bore this burden and still carried on with their responsibilities from day to day. Therefore, I say I am sure the minister is aware of that fact, as are all the other people who live in this great country of ours. We think of the high rate of taxation; we think of the constantly rising cost of living.
I received from one of my constituents just the other day a letter in which she referred
[ Mr. Patterson.]

to the efforts to increase old age pensions. This constituent referred to the fact that she was in full accord with it; she wanted it but, after all, there were many others who were facing severe difficulties because of the continual rising cost of living, and that those who are on what might be called moderate incomes were faced with very great difficulties in trying to make ends meet. This particular constituent expressed the hope that the government would come to the realization that something would have to be done to take care of this very unsatisfactory state of affairs.
Then, we think of the production of consumer goods. The other day my colleague, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), spoke along this line and referred to the fact that we are constantly hearing the statement that there is a shortage of goods. I read in a periodical the other day a reference to the $11 million that the province of Alberta is distributing as dividends to the people of that province. It said it just means that there will be $11 million more to spend on goods that we have not got. Why, bless my soul, who said that, anyway? How can they prove it? I think we all realize that our merchants are carrying on an allout campaign to sell goods. The hon. member for Macleod mentioned some of them. He did not mention some of the others, though. Nevertheless, he indicated that everywhere we look we find a tremendous sales program being carried on to dispose of goods. Yet they tell us that there is a severe shortage of goods and therefore we have to save more. I was just looking at the paper today and I saw great full-page advertisements advertising foodstuffs. May I say that foodstuffs are one of the greatest needs of our people across the country. Oh, they are buying a certain amount of foodstuffs, but if they had the money they could buy goods and food that would be better for them; it would give them a balanced diet and help them to enjoy health to a greater extent than they are enjoying it at the present time.
There are all these facts that I have mentioned. There is the demand for markets. Then, when we consider government expenditures we ask ourselves, what is the government itself doing and what is the minister doing to try to implement his own policies of saving more? I do not think there is any indication whatsoever in the budget that that is being accomplished or being attempted. Therefore, I suggest that the policy recommended by the minister of saving more will have the result, if followed, of increasing the inventories which are now on the shelves, in

the stores and in the factories. Unemployment would result; depression would come, and I know that none of us wants to see that happen.
I think the whole picture indicates that this government acts only when it is pushed hard enough; it waits not only until public opinion points out the direction, but until public sentiment becomes so insistent that to oppose it is political suicide.
In his budget speech the minister tried to leave the impression, for election purposes no doubt, that millions of Canadians are going to benefit from the provisions enunciated in the budget; but I trust that we shall all realize the benefits are so meagre that they will hardly be noticeable at all in relation to the whole economic picture across our country.
Nevertheless, we do welcome the crumbs that fall from this government's table. With an estimated production of $31J billion, and a surplus of close to $500 million, the best that this government can do is dole out a few more pence to each of our senior citizens, our disabled, our blind and our war veterans.
No wonder there is a general feeling of resentment across this country over the inadequacy of these proposals submitted and over the inability of this government to come up with a better answer to the problems that are facing us at the present time.
A great deal has been said about the tight money policy of this government and I am not going to say very much about it. We all know that our whole economy received a severe jolt when that policy was announced some time ago. We saw its effects immediately upon developments across our land. We saw its effects and we still see them in the sharp decline in house construction; it is not too much to say its effects are evident in the complete stoppage of house construction. Its effects backed up into our lumber and allied industries.
I was speaking to a lumberman just the other day and I asked him how the lumber business was. He replied that the lumber business is dead and the result is that the men engaged in lumber and sawmills and allied industries throughout the country have been thrown out of work.
We see the effects of the tight money policy in that particular relationship and we see its adverse effects on the small businesses in our country. I had the opportunity of visiting a certain area some time ago and someone told me that in a small town in that immediate vicinity there were six small businessmen who were going out of business within a week's time because
The Budget-Mr. Patterson of the effect of this government's policy or, as they might express it, the policy of the bank. Nevertheless because of the tight money policy many-yes, even hundreds- of our small businessmen are being forced to the wall and placed on the unemployment list. The policy adopted and supported by this government has had an adverse effect upon our whole national development program and our entire economy.
I would now like to speak with reference to old age pensions. We all know that concerted efforts have been made throughout the years to get the government to recognize in more adequate measure the debt we owe to our senior citizens. I do not know exactly what the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) was trying to imply in his remarks but I think he was trying to say that after all this is a provincial responsibility.
I was very glad to hear the hon. member say that old age pensioners in the province of British Columbia receive a supplemental payment of $20 a month which is the highest supplemental payment in Canada and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kootenay East, it is perhaps one of the highest paid in North America. If this federal government would come to the point where it would recognize the fact that the provincial governments and municipal authorities have obligations to fulfil and leave them a large share of the tax dollar then there would not be such a demand on the federal government. The federal government takes the lion's share of the tax dollar and when the provinces and municipalities try to discharge their responsibility they find they do not have sufficient income and are forced to come to the federal government which looks upon them with a rather paternal and patronizing attitude and says, "We will do this. We will give you this and we will give you that".
I know that we all realize the hardships confronting our senior citizens. I do not need to emphasize them nor take the time to depict the plight in which many of our senior citizens find themselves. I am sure that each hon. member of this house including the Minister of Finance is aware of their problems.
The proposal was made in the budget that old age pensions would be increased by $6 a month. I recently read a statement which appeared in the Chilliwack Progress on February 27. This was a statement made by the Chilliwack Senior Citizens' Association prior to the definite announcement that the increase would amount to $6 a month. At

The Budget-Mr. Patterson that time the rumour was that the increase would be between $5 and $10. The statement is as follows:
This branch contends that these amounts as quoted are an insult and disgrace, particularly as a large number of old age pensioners are people who years ago contributed to the present prosperity of this country.
I also have an editorial which appeared in The West Ender on February 20, 1957, a community newspaper published in the city of Vancouver. The editorial was entitled, "Will you Sell Your Vote for $5?" and although I do not intend to read the whole article I shall read the first sentence:
No doubt we should be used to Ottawa's continued and callous refusal to recognize the disastrous effect the ever-increasing cost of living is having on our old-age and veteran pensioners, but it still came as a shock to hear of the miserable five or ten dollar a month increase which has been proposed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They must feel the 5 per cent for provincial tax.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A little further down the editorial states:
To anyone who knows the amount of pressure that has been put on the government during the past three years or more, to recognize the dire need of our pensioners, it is equally sickening to see a miserly five dollar pension increase being used as vote bait for the coming election.
No thank you, Mr. St. Laurent, we are not selling our vote for five bucks.
Now, what do we find? I have read newspaper articles and received communications to the effect that at least in British Columbia and perhaps elsewhere the rents of many people in receipt of pensions of various kinds are being raised to a degree which more than offsets the increase in their pensions. It may be that the householders involved have been kind to pensioners and provided them low rental accommodation through the years. I do not know if that is the case but perhaps the situation is that now the pensioners have received an increase the landlords feel they should have an increase in the rent. In any event what is taking place results in our senior citizens and those in receipt of war veterans and disability pensions being no better off now than they were prior to the announcement being made concerning the increase in their pensions.
We have before us, Mr. Speaker, a subamendment proposed by the C.C.F. party and in a very few minutes we will be voting on that sub-amendment. As I have said we are all aware of the difficult circumstances in which many of our aged citizens find themselves. We believe that everything possible

must be done to help those who have passed their time of productive labour and because of circumstances have been unable to provide security for themselves in their later years. We in this group have always maintained that in arriving at a decision as to what these pensions should be we must take into consideration several main factors; the needs of the people, the cost of living and the productive capacity of our nation. We believe that in proposing an increase of $6 a month this government has indicated its unwillingness to consider these basic and important factors.
We are convinced that the proposed increase is not only inadequate and niggardly, it is not a true expression of the wishes of the Canadian people with respect to our senior citizens and those in the other categories named. So for these reasons we will vote for the subamendment, not because we necessarily agree that $75 is the proper rate but as a vote of protest against the inadequacy of the government proposal now before us.
As we go along in the budget speech we find that our blind citizens are going to receive consideration. There is another matter to which I should like to refer and I believe this has been referred to in other debates and in other years. I know I have mentioned it and I know many other hon. members have also. We have had requests from across the constituencies and across the country for an allowance free from a means test to take care of guiding services for our blind citizens. I have received a number of communications from Legion branches in my constituency. I have received letters from city and municipal councils asking that I support this proposal. We have had as well communications from many labour unions and individual citizens who are interested in the plight of our blind friends.
Therefore we are asking for an allowance free from a means test to take care of those special expenses which are peculiar to blindness. I do not know just why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has refused to heed this request and bring in something along this line. I suppose he has a reason; he may think it is included in or covered by the other increase proposed; but I feel that this request should have been acceded to and an allowance granted in this connection.
We have as well an announcement relative to the veterans legislation. Of course we welcome the changes that have been forecast in the budget address, but we all recognize that they are still inadequate. These changes in the veterans legislation seem to provide an outstanding example of something I have said before, that the government seems to wait until it is forced into the position where

it has to make some concession and act on the requests. We find that some of the gaps are gradually being closed, that some of the needs are being met, but all we get is a little bit at a time when the pressure seems to be so strong and so insistent that they hardly dare resist it.
We appreciate that the request has been acceded to and that the rate for married recipients of war veterans allowances is to be raised from $108 to $120. But I say again that there is still a group of veterans who are in a difficult situation. I refer to those recipients of the war veterans allowance who because of health or economic conditions in their locality are not able to supplement their incomes by casual earnings. These people are still in dire straits and they must have help. They need help and I trust that something will be brought in to improve the lot of this particular group.
We note that the permissive ceilings on earnings have been raised. In the case of a single person the request was that this ceiling should be $1,200 but the government has decided to raise it only to $950. There was a request for a $2,000 ceiling for married veterans but this now stands at $1,620. I suppose it means that the veterans will have to keep on putting on the pressure, making their requests and plugging away so that eventually the government may get around to acceding to their request in this connection.
Pensions have been raised slightly but still they are not up to what has been required and requested by the Legion in the various briefs they have presented.
There is another matter in connection with succession duties I should like to mention briefly. This is the third time there has been reference to succession duties in budget addresses of the Minister of Finance. I seem to remember that there was an indication back in 1955 that amendments to the act were being considered and would be brought in. There was a reference made to it last year and I have here a note of a question which was asked by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the reply given by the Minister of Finance was as follows:
The bill is almost ready for consultation with my colleagues. I would expect that we could have that done within the next couple of weeks. I would doubt very much if we could pass the bill at this session.
This year the minister comes along and says that he is sorry, nothing can be done; the bill is not ready and therefore nothing is going to be done in this connection. I should like to remind the minister again of the requests that have been made by many throughout the country. Two recommendations have been made, first that instead
The Budget-Mr. Patterson of exempting an estate up to $50,000 this amount be made a true exemption deductible from the value of the estate before the calculation of duties. The second is that one-half of a deceased husband's estate be considered for tax purposes as having been earned by his widow and therefor not subject to succession duties when it passed to her on his death.
Here again I suppose all we can do is to plead with the minister to give this matter consideration. If it should happen, and we certainly hope not, that he is Minister of Finance next year under a Liberal government, then we hope that consideration will be given to these matters.
There is a matter which I have brought to the attention of the minister, I think for three successive years. This has to do with deductions of donations to charitable institutions.
