speechtext:
I did not hear what the minister said; he is mumbling in his beard. We regret that the minister has not yet found it possible to grant the request I made that the rate for donations be raised to at least 20 per cent. When I mentioned this the first time the minister showed little interest. Last time he did not show very much interest. This year I do not think he is showing any interest because he thinks he has brought in a measure which takes care of the matter. I assure him that he has not.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) referred to this particular matter, but there is one thing in the hon. member's speech to which I take exception. She said :
Although tithing is now a rather outmoded form of gauging one's charitable contributions, nevertheless there are many people who, to the best of their ability, give from their earnings to charitable causes, to their churches and to other religious organizations.
I want to assure the hon. lady that there are still a great many who believe in that type of financing and who practice it. Last year I placed on the record details of the systems used in Great Britain and the United States. I shall not take time to put the details

The Budget-Mr. Patterson on record again, but I do hope the minister will look over the record and check the figures.
In the United States, up to 20 per cent of an individual's gross income paid to charitable and religious organizations may be exempted from income tax, and I think that is a reasonable basis upon which to work. The minister asked me if I did not agree with what is being done now. I think there are, possibly, two objections. One is that a great many people are going to be able to claim deductions when they do not actually turn the money over to these organizations. The other is that those persons who go beyond the 10 per cent permitted are not receiving any assistance whatsover. I think the minister should take another look at this question, and work it out. I am not saying it should be 20 per cent without vouchers; I think if we want to get credit we ought to be able to supply the vouchers from our charitable organizations. All these organizations give them, so there should be no difficulty about it.
This government professes concern for the finer things of life, and I am not saying they do not believe in those things. But I say: why not confirm that by providing this incentive to those who support these worthy causes?
Mr. Speaker, I have just one other matter to deal with. I am advised I have about five minutes left. I want to refer to the minister's statement regarding the tariff on potatoes. I am not going to read it-it is to be found at page 2224 of Hansard. We all realize the inequity of the present tariff arrangement between the United States and Canada whereby for those shipping potatoes to the United States the tariff is $7.50 a ton up to a certain amount and then is doubled at $15.00 a ton, though potatoes imported from the United States enter duty free with the exception of six weeks during the year, and that is in midsummer.
I do not know who was responsible for that. I would hate to think that even a Liberal government would accede to a proposition of that sort. But it seems this arrangement was made at some time, and it has never been changed. Concerted efforts have been made to alter it and the minister agrees that some change is desirable. In this connection I think a statement made by the acting minister of agriculture of the province of British Columbia, Mr. Kenneth Kiernan, is relevant. Referring to this situation he states that the potato tariff as it stands can bring a state of bankruptcy to the British Columbia growers.
I received in the mail today a copy of The Grower, and on page 12 we find an article headed: "Potato Growers May Stage

March on Government". These are obviously not British Columbia growers-it is too far to march, I guess. But this article states:
The potato growers of New Brunswick are up in arms. In a wire to Mr. L. F. Burrows, secretary of Canadian Horticultural Council on March 16, they said: "Our potato growers not happy since tariff on potatoes not included in budget. Talking strongly chartering train for Ottawa next week to protest. Think if U.S.A. not agreeable our government should have used escape clause. What agricultural items did U.S.A. apply tariff on under this clause? Preliminary meeting tomorrow afternoon."
With Maine potatoes flooding eastern Canada markets, and Quebec markets demoralized, the anger of the New Brunswick growers is readily understood. It is nearly two years since the Canadian potato industry asked for adjustment of the tariff on potatoes and it now looks as if the boiling point has been reached.
I sincerely hope that in the very near future negotiations which are apparently now under way will be concluded and we shall find a more favourable situation as far as tariffs are concerned, not only with respect to potatoes but also with respect to other agricultural products.

The Budget-Mr. Poulin that prices vary quite considerably from one year to the next, and even during a given production season. Under such circumstances, the producers do not know when to sell their product. They have to toss a coin-if I may use this expression-with the result that a number of them are losing vast amounts of money, because they failed to sell at the right moment. For instance, last year some producers marketed their product in the early summer for a price that was far from satisfactory to them, while probably as many others did not sell at all, and are still likely carrying their stock.
I can understand that a company, co-operative or otherwise, may be in a position to do that, but the individual producer generally cannot afford it. What complicates the situation even more is that the drums or other containers which the producer would require immediately to gather the product of the new crop are held up, thus leaving the producer in a most difficult situation.
That request for a support price has been made to me by hundreds of producers of my constituency. I will admit to the house that the granting of such a wish appeared difficult to me, and that I so stated to the Beauce constituents with the same frankness as I am stating it this evening. I explained to them the objections which, to my mind, could make the proposal impractical. I wondered for instance whether the fact of subsidizing the sale of a product, when that product is mainly sold outside of Canada, would not constitute some sort of dumping contrary to international trade regulations.
Besides,-I mean to point it out here,- my objections never were concerned with the necessity of such a measure but rather with the difficulties of carrying it out. However, I may be wrong,-I do hope I am,-and it may be that I see difficulties where there are none at all, because I am far from being an expert. I am, however, sufficiently familiar with the problem to be able at least to have doubts, and that is precisely what makes me urge the Minister of Agriculture to have this problem studied by the experts of his department. Moreover, according to a letter I received from the minister in reply to a request I made to him, I understand that the officials of his department are studying-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A motion to adjourn the debate has already been placed before the Chair by the hon. member for Lambton West and therefore I cannot accept the motion of the hon. member for Beauce.
(Translation):
I cannot accept the motion of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) since the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy)
The Budget-Division has already moved the adjournment of the debate. Since the new regulations restricting the budget debate are in effect, it has always been recognized that the member who speaks just before the vote, though it be for a mere few minutes, cannot speak immediately on the other motion which remains to be discussed. The hon. member will no doubt have the opportunity to speak later if he wishes to do so but, since he has spoken immediately before the vote on the sub-amendment, he cannot be the first to speak on the amendment.
(Text):
On motion of Mr. Murphy (Lambton West) the debate was adjourned.

Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow I shall ask that the house go into committee of ways and means in order to vote one month's supply, if the house feels so inclined.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You will ask that we go into committee of supply first, will you not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. Then we shall take the committee of supply for the estimates of the post office, and then legislation in the following order: first, the resolution concerning the conservation of north Pacific fur seals, the Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act, the Territorial Lands Act, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources Act, the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act and the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act.
